entries.5da2da7a4183a63d35dd6a7cc58c625fc6af9639: <div sID="gen18936" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="27" osisID="Ezek.27" sID="Ezek.27"/> <div eID="gen18936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18937" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18938" type="x-p"/> Still we are attending the funeral of Tyre and the lamentations made for the fall of that renowned city. In this chapter we have, I. A large account of the dignity, wealth, and splendour of Tyre, while it was in its strength, the vast trade it drove, and the interest it had among the nations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.25">ver. 1-25</reference>), which is designed to make its ruin the more lamentable. II. A prediction of its fall and ruin, and the confusion and consternation which all its neighbours shall thereby be put into, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26-Ezek.27.36">ver. 26-36</reference>. And this is intended to stain the pride of all worldly glory, and, by setting the one over-against the other, to let us see the vanity and uncertainty of the riches, honours, and pleasures of the world, and what little reason we have to place our happiness in them or to be confident of the continuance of them; so that all this is written for our learning.
entries.b82de32ebaa3394b384c2809da4c938f95d899bc: <div eID="gen18938" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18937" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prosperity of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18939" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came again unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Now, thou son of man, take up a lamentation for Tyrus; <hi type="super">3</hi> And say unto Tyrus, O thou that art situate at the entry of the sea, <hi type="italic">which art</hi> a merchant of the people for many isles, Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; O Tyrus, thou hast said, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> of perfect beauty. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thy borders <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the midst of the seas, thy builders have perfected thy beauty. <hi type="super">5</hi> They have made all thy <hi type="italic">ship</hi> boards of fir trees of Senir: they have taken cedars from Lebanon to make masts for thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> <hi type="italic">Of</hi> the oaks of Bashan have they made thine oars; the company of the Ashurites have made thy benches <hi type="italic">of</hi> ivory, <hi type="italic">brought</hi> out of the isles of Chittim. <hi type="super">7</hi> Fine linen with broidered work from Egypt was that which thou spreadest forth to be thy sail; blue and purple from the isles of Elishah was that which covered thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> The inhabitants of Zidon and Arvad were thy mariners: thy wise <hi type="italic">men,</hi> O Tyrus, <hi type="italic">that</hi> were in thee, were thy pilots. <hi type="super">9</hi> The ancients of Gebal and the wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> thereof were in thee thy calkers: all the ships of the sea with their mariners were in thee to occupy thy merchandise. <hi type="super">10</hi> They of Persia and of Lud and of Phut were in thine army, thy men of war: they hanged the shield and helmet in thee; they set forth thy comeliness. <hi type="super">11</hi> The men of Arvad with thine army <hi type="italic">were</hi> upon thy walls round about, and the Gammadims were in thy towers: they hanged their shields upon thy walls round about; they have made thy beauty perfect. <hi type="super">12</hi> Tarshish <hi type="italic">was</hi> thy merchant by reason of the multitude of all <hi type="italic">kind of</hi> riches; with silver, iron, tin, and lead, they traded in thy fairs. <hi type="super">13</hi> Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they <hi type="italic">were</hi> thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market. <hi type="super">14</hi> They of the house of Togarmah traded in thy fairs with horses and horsemen and mules. <hi type="super">15</hi> The men of Dedan <hi type="italic">were</hi> thy merchants; many isles <hi type="italic">were</hi> the merchandise of thine hand: they brought thee <hi type="italic">for</hi> a present horns of ivory and ebony. <hi type="super">16</hi> Syria <hi type="italic">was</hi> thy merchant by reason of the multitude of the wares of thy making: they occupied in thy fairs with emeralds, purple, and broidered work, and fine linen, and coral, and agate. <hi type="super">17</hi> Judah, and the land of Israel, they <hi type="italic">were</hi> thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm. <hi type="super">18</hi> Damascus <hi type="italic">was</hi> thy merchant in the multitude of the wares of thy making, for the multitude of all riches; in the wine of Helbon, and white wool. <hi type="super">19</hi> Dan also and Javan going to and fro occupied in thy fairs: bright iron, cassia, and calamus, were in thy market. <hi type="super">20</hi> Dedan <hi type="italic">was</hi> thy merchant in precious clothes for chariots. <hi type="super">21</hi> Arabia, and all the princes of Kedar, they occupied with thee in lambs, and rams, and goats: in these <hi type="italic">were they</hi> thy merchants. <hi type="super">22</hi> The merchants of Sheba and Raamah, they <hi type="italic">were</hi> thy merchants: they occupied in thy fairs with chief of all spices, and with all precious stones, and gold. <hi type="super">23</hi> Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Chilmad, <hi type="italic">were</hi> thy merchants. <hi type="super">24</hi> These <hi type="italic">were</hi> thy merchants in all sorts <hi type="italic">of things,</hi> in blue clothes, and broidered work, and in chests of rich apparel, bound with cords, and made of cedar, among thy merchandise. <hi type="super">25</hi> The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas. <div eID="gen18939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18940" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prophet is ordered to take up a lamentation for Tyrus, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.2">v. 2</reference>. It was yet in the height of its prosperity, and there appeared not the least symptom of its decay; yet the prophet must lament it, because its prosperity is its snare, is the cause of its pride and security, which will make its fall the more grievous. Even those that live at ease are to be lamented if they be not preparing for trouble. He must lament it because its ruin is hastening on apace; it is sure, it is near; and though the prophet foretel it, and justify God in it, yet he must lament it. Note, We ought to mourn for the miseries of other nations, as well as for our own, out of an affection for mankind in general; it is a part of the honour we owe to all men to bewail their calamities, even those which they have brought upon themselves by their own folly. <div eID="gen18940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18941" type="x-p"/> II. He is directed what to say, and to say it in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord Jehovah,</hi> a name not unknown in Tyre, and which shall be better known, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.6">ch. xxvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen18941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18942" type="x-p"/> 1. He must upbraid Tyre with her pride: <hi type="italic">O Tyrus! thou hast said, I am of perfect beauty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">v. 3</reference>), of <hi type="italic">universal beauty</hi> (so the word is), every way accomplished, and therefore every where admired. Zion, that had the <hi type="italic">beauty of holiness,</hi> is called indeed the <hi type="italic">perfection of beauty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Ps. l. 2</reference>); that is the <hi type="italic">beauty of the Lord.</hi> But Tyre, because well-built and well-filled with money and trade, will set up for a perfect beauty. Note, It is the folly of the children of this world to value themselves on the pomp and pleasure they live in, to call themselves beauties for the sake of them, and, if in these they excel others, to think themselves perfect. But God takes notice of the vain conceits men have of themselves in their prosperity when the mind is lifted up with the condition, and often, for the humbling of the spirit, finds a way to bring down the estate. Let none reckon themselves beautified any further than they are sanctified, nor say that they are of perfect beauty till they come to heaven. <div eID="gen18942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18943" type="x-p"/> 2. He must upbraid Tyre with her prosperity, which was the matter of her pride. In elegies it is usual to insert encomiums of those whose fall we lament; the prophet, accordingly, praises Tyre for all that she had that was praiseworthy. He has nothing to say of her religion, her piety, her charity, her being a refuge to the distressed or using her interest to do good offices among her neighbours; but she lived great, and had a great trade, and all the trading part of mankind made court to her. The prophet must describe her height and magnificence, that God may be the more glorified in her fall, as the God who <hi type="italic">looks upon every one that is proud and abases him, hides the proud in the dust together, and binds their faces in secret,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.12">Job xl. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen18943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18944" type="x-p"/> (1.) The city of Tyre was advantageously situated, <hi type="italic">at the entry of the sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">v. 3</reference>), having many commodious harbours each way, not as cities seated on rivers, which the shipping can come but one way to. It stood at the east end of the Mediterranean, very convenient for trade by land into all the Levant parts; so that she became a <hi type="italic">merchant of the people for many isles.</hi> Lying between Greece and Asia, it became the great emporium, or mart-town, the rendezvous of merchants from all parts: <hi type="italic">They borders are in the heart of the seas,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">v. 4</reference>. It was surrounded with water, which was a great advantage to its trade; it was the darling of the sea, laid in its bosom, in its heart. Note, It is a great convenience, upon many accounts, to live in an island: seas are the most <hi type="italic">ancient land-mark,</hi> not <hi type="italic">which our fathers have set,</hi> but the God of our fathers, and which cannot be removed as other land-marks may, nor so easily got over. The people so situated may the more easily <hi type="italic">dwell alone,</hi> if they please, as <hi type="italic">not reckoned among the nations,</hi> and yet, if they please, may the more easily traffic abroad and keep a correspondence with the nations. We therefore of this island must own that he who determines the bounds of men's habitations has determined well for us. <div eID="gen18944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18945" type="x-p"/> (2.) It was curiously built, according as the fashion then was; and, being a city on a hill, it made a glorious show and tempted the ships that sailed by into her ports (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy builders have perfected thy beauty;</hi> they have so improved in architecture that nothing appears in the buildings of Tyre that can be found fault with; and yet it wants that perfection of beauty into which the Lord does and will build up his Jerusalem. <div eID="gen18945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18946" type="x-p"/> (3.) It had its haven replenished with abundance of <hi type="italic">gallant ships,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa. xxxiii. 21</reference>. The ship-carpenters did their part, as well as the house-carpenters theirs. The Tyrians are thought to be the first that invented the art of navigation; at least they improved it, and brought it to as great a perfection perhaps as it could be without the loadstone. [1.] They made the <hi type="italic">boards,</hi> or planks, for the hulk of the ship, of <hi type="italic">fir-trees</hi> fetched from <hi type="italic">Senir,</hi> a mount in the land of Israel, joined with Hermon, <reference osisRef="Song.4.8">Cant. iv. 8</reference>. Planks of fir were smooth and light, but not so lasting as our English oak. [2.] They had cedars from Lebanon, another mountain of Israel, for their masts, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.5">v. 5</reference>. [3.] They had oaks from Bashan (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.13">Isa. ii. 13</reference>), to make oars of; for it is probable that their ships were mostly galleys, that go with oars. The people of Israel built few ships for themselves, but they furnished the Tyrians with timber for shipping. Thus one country uses what another produced, and so they are serviceable one to another, and cannot say to each other, <hi type="italic">I have no need of thee.</hi> [4.] Such magnificence did they affect in building their ships that they made the very <hi type="italic">benches</hi> of <hi type="italic">ivory,</hi> which they fetched from <hi type="italic">the isles of Chittim,</hi> from Italy or Greece, and had workmen from the Ashurites or Assyrians to make them, so rich would they have their state-rooms in their ships to be. [5.] So very prodigal were they that they made their <hi type="italic">sails</hi> of <hi type="italic">fine linen</hi> fetched from Egypt, and that <hi type="italic">embroidered</hi> too, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.7">v. 7</reference>. Or it may be meant of their <hi type="italic">flags</hi> (which they hoisted to notify what city they belonged to), which were very costly. The word signifies a <hi type="italic">banner</hi> as well as a <hi type="italic">sail.</hi> [6.] They hung those rooms on ship-board with <hi type="italic">blue and purple,</hi> the richest cloths and richest colours they could get from the isles they traded with. For though Tyre was itself famous for purple, which is therefore called the <hi type="italic">Tyrian dye,</hi> yet they must have that which was far-fetched. <div eID="gen18946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18947" type="x-p"/> (4.) These gallant ships were well-manned, by men of great ingenuity and industry. The pilots and masters of the ships, that had command in their fleets, were of their own city, such as they could put a confidence in (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy wise men, O Tyrus! that were in thee, were thy pilots.</hi> But, for common sailors, they had men from other countries; <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Arvad and Zidon were thy mariners.</hi> These came from cities hear them; Zidon was sister to Tyre, not two leagues off, to the northward; there they bred able seamen, which it is the interest of the maritime powers to support and give all the countenance they can to. They sent to Gebal in Syria for <hi type="italic">calkers,</hi> or <hi type="italic">strengtheners of the clefts</hi> or <hi type="italic">chinks,</hi> to stop them when the ships come home, after long voyages, to be repaired. To do this they had the <hi type="italic">ancients</hi> and <hi type="italic">wise men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.9">v. 9</reference>); for there is more need of wisdom and prudence to repair what has gone to decay than to build anew. In public matters there is occasion for the <hi type="italic">ancients</hi> and <hi type="italic">wise men</hi> to be the <hi type="italic">repairers of the breaches and the restorers of paths to dwell in.</hi> Nay, all the countries they traded with were at their service, and were willing to send men into their pay, to put their youths apprentice in Tyre, or to put them on board their fleets; so that <hi type="italic">all the ships in the sea with their mariners were</hi> ready <hi type="italic">to occupy thy merchandise.</hi> Those that give good wages shall have hands at command. <div eID="gen18947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18948" type="x-p"/> (5.) Their city was guarded by a military force that was very considerable, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10-Ezek.27.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. The Tyrians were themselves wholly given to trade; but it was necessary that they should have a good army on foot, and therefore they took those of other states into their pay, such as were fittest for service, though they had them from afar (which perhaps was their policy), from Persia, Lud, and Phut. These bore their arms when there was occasion, and in time of peace <hi type="italic">hung up the shield and buckler</hi> in the armoury, as it were to proclaim peace, and let the world know that they had at present no need of them, but they were ready to be taken down whenever there was occasion for them. Their <hi type="italic">walls</hi> were <hi type="italic">guarded</hi> by the <hi type="italic">man of Arvad;</hi> their <hi type="italic">towers</hi> were garrisoned by <hi type="italic">the Gammadim,</hi> robust men, that had a great deal of strength in <hi type="italic">their arms;</hi> yet the vulgar Latin renders it <hi type="italic">pygmies,</hi> men no longer than one's arm. They <hi type="italic">hung their shields upon the walls</hi> in their magazines or places of arms; or hung them out upon the walls of the city, that none might dare to approach them, seeing how well provided they were with all things necessary for their own defence. "Thus <hi type="italic">they set forth thy comeliness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">v. 10</reference>), and <hi type="italic">made they beauty perfect,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.11">v. 11</reference>. It contributed as much as any thing to the glory of Tyre that it had those of all the surrounding nations in its service, except the land of Israel (though it lay next them), which furnished them with timber, but we do not find that it furnished them with men; that would have trenched upon the liberty and dignity of the Jewish nation, <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.17-2Chr.2.18">2 Chron. ii. 17, 18</reference>. It was also the glory of Tyre that it had such a militia, so fit for service, and in constant pay, and such an armoury, like that in the tower of David, where hung the <hi type="italic">shields of mighty men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.4">Cant. iv. 4</reference>. It is observable that there and here the armouries are said to be furnished with <hi type="italic">shields</hi> and <hi type="italic">helmets,</hi> defensive arms, not with swords and spears, offensive, though it is probable that there were such, to intimate that the military force of a people must be intended only for their own protection and not to invade and annoy their neighbours, to secure their own right, not to encroach upon the rights of others. <div eID="gen18948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18949" type="x-p"/> (6.) They had a vast trade and a correspondence with all parts of the known world. Some nations they dealt with in one commodity and some in another, according as either its products or its manufactures were, and the fruits of nature or art were, with which it was blessed. This is very much enlarged upon here, as that which was the principal glory of Tyre, and which supported all the rest. We do not find any where in scripture so many nations named together as are here; so that this chapter, some think, gives much light to the first account we have of the settlement of the nations after the flood, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.1-Gen.10.32">Gen. x</reference>. The critics have abundance of work here to find out the several places and nations spoken of. Concerning many of them their conjectures are different and they leave us in the dark and at much uncertainty; it is well that it is not material. Modern surveys come short of explaining the ancient geography. And therefore we will not amuse ourselves here with a particular enquiry either concerning the traders or the goods they traded in. We leave it to the critical expositors, and observe that only which is improvable. [1.] We have reason to think that Ezekiel knew little, of his own knowledge, concerning the trade of Tyre. He was a priest, carried away captive far enough from the neighbourhood of Tyre, we may suppose when he was young, and there he had been eleven years. And yet he speaks of the particular merchandises of Tyre as nicely as if he had been comptroller of the custom-house there, by which it appears that he was divinely inspired in what he spoke and wrote. It is God that <hi type="italic">saith this,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">v. 3</reference>. [2.] This account of the trade of Tyre intimates to us that God's eye is upon men, and that he takes cognizance of what they do when they are employed in their worldly business, not only when they are at church, praying and hearing, but when they are in their markets and fairs, and upon the exchange, buying and selling, which is a good reason why we should in all our dealings <hi type="italic">keep a conscience void of offence,</hi> and have our eye always upon him whose eye is always upon us. [3.] We may here observe the wisdom of God, and his goodness, as the common Father of mankind, in making one country to abound in one commodity and another in another, and all more or less serviceable either to the necessity or to the comfort or ornament of human life. <hi type="italic">Non omis fert omnia tellus—One land does not supply all the varieties of produce.</hi> Providence dispenses its gifts variously, some to each, and all to none, that there may be a mutual commerce among those whom God has <hi type="italic">made of one blood,</hi> though they are made <hi type="italic">to dwell on all the face of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.17.27">Acts xvii. 26</reference>. Let every nations therefore thank God for the productions of its country; though they be not so rich as those of others, yet there is use for them in the public service of the world. [4.] See what a blessing trade and merchandise are to mankind, especially when followed in the fear of God, and with a regard not only to private advantage, but to a common benefit. <hi type="italic">The earth is full of God's riches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.24">Ps. civ. 24</reference>. There is a <hi type="italic">multitude of all kinds of riches</hi> in it (as it is here, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12">v. 12</reference>), gathered off its surface and dug out of its bowels. The earth is also full of the fruits of men's ingenuity and industry, according as their genius leads them. Now by exchange and barter these are made more extensively useful; thus what can be spared is helped off, and what is wanted is fetched in, in lieu of it, from the most distant countries. Those that are not tradesmen themselves have reason to thank God for tradesmen and merchants, by whom the productions of other countries are brought to our hands, as those of our own are by our husbandmen. [5.] Besides the necessaries that are here traded in, see what abundance of things are here mentioned that only serve to please fancy, and are made valuable only by men's humour and custom; and yet God allows us to use them, and trade in them, and part with those things for them which we can spare that are of an intrinsic worth much beyond them. Here are <hi type="italic">horns of ivory and ebony</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">v. 15</reference>), that are <hi type="italic">brought for a present,</hi> exposed to sale, and offered in exchange, or (as some think) presented to the city, or the great men of it, to obtain their favour. Here are <hi type="italic">emeralds, coral,</hi> and <hi type="italic">agate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">v. 16</reference>), all <hi type="italic">precious stones, and gold</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.22">v. 22</reference>), which the world could better be without than iron and common stones. Here are, to please the taste and smell, the <hi type="italic">chief of all spices</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.22">v. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">cassia and calamus</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.19">v. 19</reference>), and, for ornament, <hi type="italic">purple, broidered work, and fine linen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">precious clothes for chariots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">blue clothes</hi> (which Tyre was famous for), <hi type="italic">broidered work,</hi> and <hi type="italic">chests of rich apparel, bound with</hi> rich <hi type="italic">cords,</hi> and <hi type="italic">made of cedar,</hi> a sweet wood to perfume the garments kept in them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.24">v. 24</reference>. Upon the review of this invoice, or bill of parcels, we may justly say, What a great many things are here that we have no need of, and can live very comfortably without! [6.] It is observable that Judah and the <hi type="italic">land of Israel</hi> were merchants in Tyre too; in a way of trade they were allowed to converse with the heathen. But they traded mostly <hi type="italic">in wheat,</hi> a substantial commodity, and necessary, <hi type="italic">wheat of Minnith and Pannag,</hi> two countries in Canaan famous for the best wheat, as some think. The whole land indeed was a <hi type="italic">land of wheat</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.8">Deut. viii. 8</reference>); it had <hi type="italic">the fat of kidneys of wheat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">Deut. xxxii. 14</reference>. Tyre was maintained by corn fetched from the land of Israel. They traded likewise in <hi type="italic">honey, and oil,</hi> and <hi type="italic">balm,</hi> or <hi type="italic">rosin;</hi> all useful things, and not serving to pride or luxury. And the land which these were the staple commodities of was that which was the <hi type="italic">glory of all lands,</hi> which God reserved for his peculiar people, not those that traded in spices and <hi type="italic">precious stones;</hi> and the Israel of God must reckon themselves well provided for if they have <hi type="italic">food convenient;</hi> for those that are acquainted with the delights of the children of God will not set their hearts on the <hi type="italic">delights of the sons and daughters of men,</hi> or the <hi type="italic">treasures of kings and provinces.</hi> We find indeed that the New-Testament Babylon trades in such things as Tyre traded in, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.12-Rev.18.13">Rev. xviii. 12, 13</reference>. For, notwithstanding its pretensions to sanctity, it is a mere worldly interest. [7.] Though Tyre was a city of great merchandise, and they got abundance by buying and selling, importing commodities from one place and exporting them to another, yet manufacture-trades were not neglected. The <hi type="italic">wares of their own making,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">multitude of such wares,</hi> are here spoken of, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">v. 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.18">18</reference>. It is the wisdom of a nation to encourage art and industry, and not to bear hard upon the handicraft-tradesmen; for it contributes much to the wealth and honour of a nation to send abroad <hi type="italic">wares of their own making,</hi> which may bring them in the <hi type="italic">multitude of all riches.</hi> [8.] All this made Tyrus very great and very proud: <hi type="italic">The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in they market</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.25">v. 25</reference>); thou wast admired and cried up by all the nations that had dealings with thee; for <hi type="italic">thou wast replenished</hi> in wealth and number of people, wast beautified, and <hi type="italic">made very glorious, in the midst of the seas.</hi> Those that grow very rich are cried up as very glorious; for riches are glorious things in the eyes of carnal people, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.1">Gen. xxxi. 1</reference>.
entries.5a904ffb62c1383a9e70c106a743a3b8f1afe96d: <div eID="gen18949" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Fall of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18950" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters: the east wind hath broken thee in the midst of the seas. <hi type="super">27</hi> Thy riches, and thy fairs, thy merchandise, thy mariners, and thy pilots, thy calkers, and the occupiers of thy merchandise, and all thy men of war, that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in thee, and in all thy company which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the midst of thee, shall fall into the midst of the seas in the day of thy ruin. <hi type="super">28</hi> The suburbs shall shake at the sound of the cry of thy pilots. <hi type="super">29</hi> And all that handle the oar, the mariners, <hi type="italic">and</hi> all the pilots of the sea, shall come down from their ships, they shall stand upon the land; <hi type="super">30</hi> And shall cause their voice to be heard against thee, and shall cry bitterly, and shall cast up dust upon their heads, they shall wallow themselves in the ashes: <hi type="super">31</hi> And they shall make themselves utterly bald for thee, and gird them with sackcloth, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart <hi type="italic">and</hi> bitter wailing. <hi type="super">32</hi> And in their wailing they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> What <hi type="italic">city is</hi> like Tyrus, like the destroyed in the midst of the sea? <hi type="super">33</hi> When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise. <hi type="super">34</hi> In the time <hi type="italic">when</hi> thou shalt be broken by the seas in the depths of the waters thy merchandise and all thy company in the midst of thee shall fall. <hi type="super">35</hi> All the inhabitants of the isles shall be astonished at thee, and their kings shall be sore afraid, they shall be troubled in <hi type="italic">their</hi> countenance. <hi type="super">36</hi> The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee; thou shalt be a terror, and never <hi type="italic">shalt be</hi> any more. <div eID="gen18950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18951" type="x-p"/> We have seen Tyre flourishing; here we have Tyre falling, and great is the fall of it, so much the greater for its having made such a figure in the world. Note, The most mighty and magnificent kingdoms and states, sooner or later, have their day to come down. They have their period; and, when they are in their zenith, they will begin to decline. But the destruction of Tyre was sudden. Her <hi type="italic">sun went down at noon.</hi> And all her wealth and grandeur, pomp and power, did but aggravate her ruin, and make it the more grievous to herself and astonishing to all about her. Now observe here, 1. How the ruin of Tyrus will be brought about, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26">v. 26</reference>. She is as a great ship richly laden, that is split or sunk by the indiscretion of her steersmen: <hi type="italic">Thy rowers have</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">brought thee into great</hi> and dangerous <hi type="italic">waters;</hi> the governors of the city, and those that had the management of their public affairs, by some mismanagement or other involved them in that war with the Chaldeans which was the ruin of their state. By their insolence, by some affront given to the Chaldeans or some attempt made upon them, in confidence of their own ability to contend with them, they provoked Nebuchadnezzar to make a descent upon them, and, by their obstinacy in standing it out to the last, enraged him to such a degree that he determined on the ruin of their state, and, <hi type="italic">like an east wind, broke them in the midst of the seas.</hi> Note, It is ill with a people when those that sit at the stern, instead of putting them into the harbour, run them aground. 2. How great and general the ruin will be. All her wealth shall be buried with her, <hi type="italic">her riches, her fairs, and her merchandise</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.27">v. 27</reference>); all that had any dependence upon her, and dealings with her, in trade, in war, in conversation, shall <hi type="italic">ball with her into the midst of the seas, in the day of her ruin.</hi> Note, Those who make creatures their confidence, place their happiness in their interest in them and rest their hopes upon them, will of course fall with them; <hi type="italic">happy</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">are those that have the God of Jacob for their help,</hi> and <hi type="italic">whose hope is in the Lord their God,</hi> who lives for ever. 3. What sad lamentation would be made for the destruction of Tyre. The pilots, her princes and governors, when they see how wretchedly they have mismanaged and how much they have contributed to their own ruin, shall <hi type="italic">cry out</hi> so loud as to make even the <hi type="italic">suburbs shake</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.28">v. 28</reference>), such a vexation shall it be to them to reflect upon their own bad conduct. The inferior officers, that were as the mariners of the state, shall be forced to come down from their respective posts (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.29">v. 29</reference>), and they shall <hi type="italic">cry out against thee,</hi> as having deceived them, in not proving so well able to hold out as they thought thou hadst been; they shall <hi type="italic">cry bitterly</hi> for the common ruin, and their own share in it. They shall use all the most solemn expressions of grief; they shall <hi type="italic">cast dust on their heads,</hi> in indignation against themselves, shall <hi type="italic">wallow themselves in ashes,</hi> as having bid a final farewell to all ease and pleasure; they shall <hi type="italic">make themselves bald</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.31">v. 31</reference>), with <hi type="italic">tearing their hair;</hi> and, according to the custom of great mourners, those shall <hi type="italic">gird themselves with sackcloth</hi> who used to wear fine linen, and, instead of merry songs, they shall <hi type="italic">weep with bitterness of heart.</hi> Note, Losses and crosses are very grievous, and hard to be borne, to those that have long been wallowing in pleasure and sleeping in carnal security. 4. How Tyre should be upbraided with her former honour and prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.32-Ezek.27.33">v. 32, 33</reference>); she that was Tyrus the <hi type="italic">renowned</hi> shall now be called <hi type="italic">Tyrus the destroyed</hi> in the <hi type="italic">midst of the sea. "What city is like Tyre?</hi> Did ever any city come down from such a height of prosperity to such a depth of adversity? Time was when <hi type="italic">thy wares,</hi> those of thy own making and those that passed through thy hands, <hi type="italic">went forth out of the seas,</hi> and were exported to all parts of the world; then <hi type="italic">thou filledst many people,</hi> and didst <hi type="italic">enrich the kings of the earth</hi> and their kingdoms." The Tyrians, though they bore such a sway in trade, were yet, it seems, fair merchants, and let their neighbours not only live, but thrive by them. All that dealt with them were gainers; they did not cheat or oppress the people, but did enrich them with <hi type="italic">the multitude of their merchandise.</hi> "But now those that used to be enriched by thee shall be ruined with thee" (as is usual in trade); "<hi type="italic">when thou shalt be broken,</hi> and all thou hast is seized on, <hi type="italic">all thy company shall fall too,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.34">v. 34</reference>. There is an end of Tyre, that made such a noise and bustle in the world. This great blaze goes out in a snuff. 5. How the fall of Tyre should be matter of terror to some and laughter to others, according as they were differently interested and affected. Some shall be <hi type="italic">sorely afraid,</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">be troubled</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.35">v. 35</reference>), concluding it will be their own turn to fall next. Others shall <hi type="italic">hiss at her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.36">v. 36</reference>), shall ridicule her pride, and vanity, and bad management, and think her ruin just. She triumphed in Jerusalem's fall, and there are those that will triumph in hers. When God casts his judgments on the sinner <hi type="italic">men</hi> also <hi type="italic">shall clap their hands at him</hi> and <hi type="italic">shall hiss him out of his place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.22-Job.27.23">Job xxvii. 22, 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Is this the city which men called the perfection of beauty?</hi>  <chapter eID="Ezek.27"/> <div eID="gen18951" type="x-p"/>

entries.7be8e4270a0b939257eac4ac4799a711e72291cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11518"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 27</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:1-36</reference>. Tyre's Former Greatness, Suggesting a Lamentation over Her Sad Downfall.</title> <div sID="gen20847" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11518"/><hi type="bold">2. lamentation--</hi>a funeral dirge, eulogizing her great attributes, to make the contrast the greater between her former and her latter state. <div eID="gen20847" type="x-p"/>
entries.92274185c283106c53e3e222270054a3c6ab9ae9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11519"/><div sID="gen20848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11519"/><hi type="bold">3. situate at the entry of the sea--</hi>literally, plural, "entrances," that is, ports or havens; referring to the double port of Tyre, at which vessels entered round the north and south ends of the island, so that ships could find a ready entrance from whatever point the wind might blow (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Eze 28:2</reference>).<div eID="gen20848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20849" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">merchant of ... people for many isles--</hi>that is, a mercantile emporium of the peoples of many seacoasts, both from the east and from the west (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.3">Is 23:3</reference>), "a mart of nations."<div eID="gen20849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of perfect beauty--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.12">Eze 28:12</reference>). <div eID="gen20850" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f3c9deff3cf3fe67903a4c03047aff366d4d404: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11520"/><div sID="gen20851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11520"/>4. Tyre, in consonance with her seagirt position, separated by a strait of half a mile from the mainland, is described as a ship built of the best material, and manned with the best mariners and skilful pilots, but at last wrecked in tempestuous seas (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26">Eze 27:26</reference>). <div eID="gen20851" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c4bda211fbf993b787e3bb5931a0337640d95be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11521"/><div sID="gen20852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11521"/><hi type="bold">5. Senir--</hi>the Amorite name of Hermon, or the southern height of Anti-libanus (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">De 3:9</reference>); the Sidonian name was Sirion. "All thy ... boards"; dual in Hebrew, "double-boards," namely, placed in a double order on the two sides of which the ship consisted [Vatablus]. Or, referring to the two sides or the two ends, the prow and the stern, which every ship has [Munster].<div eID="gen20852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cedars--</hi>most suited for "masts," from their height and durability. <div eID="gen20853" type="x-p"/>
entries.28d36da85929f261a7542c3a3609b7cb86ee932e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11522"/><div sID="gen20854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11522"/><hi type="bold">6. Bashan--</hi>celebrated for its oaks, as Lebanon was for its cedars.<div eID="gen20854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20855" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the company of ... Ashurites--</hi>the most skilful workmen summoned from Assyria. Rather, as the Hebrew orthography requires, "They have made thy (rowing) benches of ivory inlaid in the daughter of cedars" [Maurer], or, the best boxwood. Fairbairn, with Bochart, reads the Hebrew two words as one: "Thy plankwork (deck: instead of 'benches,' as the Hebrew is singular) they made ivory with boxes." English Version, with Maurer's correction, is simpler.<div eID="gen20855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chittim--</hi>Cyprus and Macedonia, from which, Pliny tells us, the best boxwood came [Grotius]. <div eID="gen20856" type="x-p"/>
entries.da80ba9fcbfabeba06900b9276383bdc368d09b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11523"/><div sID="gen20857" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11523"/><hi type="bold">7. broidered ... sail--</hi>The ancients embroidered their sails often at great expense, especially the Egyptians, whose linen, still preserved in mummies, is of the finest texture.<div eID="gen20857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Elishah--</hi>Greece; so called from Elis, a large and ancient division of Peloponnesus. Pausanias says that the best of linen was produced in it, and in no other part of Greece; called by Homer, Alisium.<div eID="gen20858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20859" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which covered thee--</hi>thy awning. <div eID="gen20859" type="x-p"/>
entries.39293e3e0f279caaca288cd456d456a7f7f99573: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11524"/><div sID="gen20860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11524"/><hi type="bold">8. Arvad--</hi>a small island and city near Phoenicia, now Ruad: its inhabitants are still noted for seafaring habits.<div eID="gen20860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy wise men, O Tyrus ... thy pilots--</hi>While the men of Arvad, once thy equals (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.18">Ge 10:18</reference>), and the Sidonians, once thy superiors, were employed by thee in subordinate positions as "mariners," thou madest thine own skilled men alone to be commanders and pilots. Implying the political and mercantile superiority of Tyre. <div eID="gen20861" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9c04fa57ecfeef14769b8aa0e2bb900383c6d38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11525"/><div sID="gen20862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11525"/><hi type="bold">9. Gebal--</hi>a Phoenician city and region between Beirut and Tripolis, famed for skilled workmen (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.18">1Ki 5:18</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.7">Psa 83:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calkers--</hi>stoppers of chinks in a vessel: carrying on the metaphor as to Tyre.<div eID="gen20863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occupy thy merchandise--</hi>that is, to exchange merchandise with thee. <div eID="gen20864" type="x-p"/>
entries.68339c8ba1de8dece7bf1a74ecd2869df3546909: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11526"/><div sID="gen20865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11526"/><hi type="bold">10. Persia ... Phut--</hi>warriors from the extreme east and west.<div eID="gen20865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lud--</hi>the Lydians of Asia Minor, near the Meander, famed for archery (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>); rather than those of Ethiopia, as the Lydians of Asia Minor form a kind of intermediate step between Persia and Phut (the Libyans about Cyrene, shielded warriors, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jr 46:9</reference>, descended from Phut, son of Ham).<div eID="gen20866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hanged ... shield ... comeliness--</hi>Warriors hanged their accoutrements on the walls for ornament. Divested of the metaphor, it means that it was an honor to thee to have so many nations supplying thee with hired soldiers. <div eID="gen20867" type="x-p"/>
entries.96c78a0e9242f2b3c54f2fe9ce6ef866b3e07d6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11527"/><div sID="gen20868" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11527"/><hi type="bold">11. Gammadims--</hi>rather, as the Tyrians were Syro-Phoenicians, from a Syriac root, meaning daring, "men of daring" [Ludovicus De Dieu]. It is not likely the keeping of watch "in the towers" would have been entrusted to foreigners. Others take it from a Hebrew root, "a dagger," or short sword (<reference osisRef="Judg.3.16">Jud 3:16</reference>), "short-swordsmen." <div eID="gen20868" type="x-p"/>
entries.17b3d39ea77ea591b34231220f12a01a22dd9f80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11528"/><div sID="gen20869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11528"/><hi type="bold">12. Tarshish--</hi>Tartessus in Spain, a country famed for various metals, which were exported to Tyre. Much of the "tin" probably was conveyed by the Phoenicians from Cornwall to Tarshish.<div eID="gen20869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">traded in thy fairs--</hi>"did barter with thee" [Fairbairn]; from a root, "to leave," something left in barter for something else. <div eID="gen20870" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb149b349745d88cfd52b76e5555c10497827f1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11529"/><div sID="gen20871" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11529"/><hi type="bold">13. Javan--</hi>the Ionians or Greeks: for the Ionians of Asia Minor were the first Greeks with whom the Asiatics came in contact.<div eID="gen20871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tubal ... Meshech--</hi>the Tibareni and Moschi, in the mountain region between the Black and Caspian Seas.<div eID="gen20872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20873" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">persons of men--</hi>that is, as slaves. So the Turkish harems are supplied with female slaves from Circassia and Georgia.<div eID="gen20873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vessels--</hi>all kinds of articles. Superior weapons are still manufactured in the Caucasus region. <div eID="gen20874" type="x-p"/>
entries.63b899435a2311cc093030bdded744652a624d56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11530"/><div sID="gen20875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11530"/><hi type="bold">14. Togarmah--</hi>Armenia: descended from Gomer (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.3">Ge 10:3</reference>). Their mountainous region south of the Caucasus was celebrated for horses.<div eID="gen20875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20876" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horsemen--</hi>rather, "riding-horses," as distinct from "horses" for chariots [Fairbairn]. <div eID="gen20876" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d027a6236649c2eb54be68e62159b2476e0478e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11531"/><div sID="gen20877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11531"/><hi type="bold">15. Dedan--</hi>near the Persian Sea: thus an avenue to the commerce of India. Not the Dedan in Arabia (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">Eze 27:20</reference>), as the names in the context here prove, but the Dedan sprung from Cush [Bochart], (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Ge 10:7</reference>).<div eID="gen20877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">merchandise of thine hand--</hi>that is, were dependent on thee for trade [Fairbairn]; came to buy the produce of thy hands [Grotius].<div eID="gen20878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a present--</hi>literally, "a reward in return"; a price paid for merchandise.<div eID="gen20879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horns of ivory--</hi>Ivory is so termed from its resemblance to horns. The Hebrew word for "ivory" means "tooth"; so that they cannot have mistaken ivory as if coming from the horns of certain animals, instead of from the tusks of the elephant. <div eID="gen20880" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ee88ea860bd766123539e692d8197304187475f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11532"/><div sID="gen20881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11532"/>16. "Syria was thy mart for the multitude," &c. For "Syria" the Septuagint reads "Edom." But the Syrians were famed as merchants.<div eID="gen20881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occupied--</hi>old English for "traded"; so in <reference osisRef="Luke.19.13">Lu 19:13</reference>.<div eID="gen20882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">agate--</hi>Others translate, "ruby," "chalcedony," or "pearls." <div eID="gen20883" type="x-p"/>
entries.db4995e228b4f1e6228b62b80bd0ed461a3600c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11533"/><div sID="gen20884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11533"/><hi type="bold">17. Minnith ... Pannag--</hi>names of places in Israel famed for good wheat, wherewith Tyre was supplied (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.9">1Ki 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.7">Ezr 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.20">Ac 12:20</reference>); Minnith was formerly an Ammonite city (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.33">Jud 11:33</reference>). "Pannag" is identified by Grotius with "Phenice," the Greek name for "Canaan." "They traded ... wheat," that is, they supplied thy market with wheat.<div eID="gen20884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">balm--</hi>or, "balsam." <div eID="gen20885" type="x-p"/>
entries.d190c604978a6d09bcda89e23358661455a94f5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11534"/><div sID="gen20886" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11534"/><hi type="bold">18. Helbon--</hi>or Chalybon, in Syria, now Aleppo; famed for its wines; the Persian monarchs would drink no other. <div eID="gen20886" type="x-p"/>
entries.10c9c6638b24f544acdcfbc6d455069f6c83335e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11535"/><div sID="gen20887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11535"/><hi type="bold">19. Dan also--</hi>None of the other places enumerated commence with the copula ("also"; Hebrew, ve). Moreover, the products specified, "cassia, calamus," apply rather to places in Arabia. Therefore, Fairbairn translates, "Vedan"; perhaps the modern Aden, near the straits of Bab-el-man-deb. Grotius refers it to Dana, mentioned by Ptolemy.<div eID="gen20887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20888" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Javan--</hi>not the Greeks of Europe or Asia Minor, but of a Greek settlement in Arabia.<div eID="gen20888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20889" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">going to and fro--</hi>rather, as Hebrew admits, "from Uzal." This is added to "Javan," to mark which Javan is meant (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.27">Ge 10:27</reference>). The metropolis of Arabia Felix, or Yemen; called also Sanaa [Bochart]. English Version gives a good sense, thus: All peoples, whether near as the Israelite "Dan," or far as the Greeks or "Javan," who were wont to "go to and fro" from their love of traffic, frequented thy marts, bringing bright iron, &c., these products not being necessarily represented as those of Dan or Javan.<div eID="gen20889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bright iron--</hi>Yemen is still famed for its sword blades.<div eID="gen20890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calamus--</hi>aromatic cane. <div eID="gen20891" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bb15a9af96ae5039612054d248f4fb19b6af751: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11536"/><div sID="gen20892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11536"/><hi type="bold">20. Dedan--</hi>in Arabia; distinct from the Dedan in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference>). Descended from Abraham and Keturah (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Ge 25:3</reference>) [Bochart].<div eID="gen20892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">precious clothes--</hi>splendid coverlets. <div eID="gen20893" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e1841ea8a34e859f6fd4663107ee29db26d3aae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11537"/><div sID="gen20894" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11537"/><hi type="bold">21. Arabia--</hi>the nomadic tribes of Arabia, among which Kedar was pre-eminent.<div eID="gen20894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">occupied with thee--</hi>literally, "of thy hand," that is, they traded with thee for wares, the product of thy hand (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen20895" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e7459e75c112060f48a42871713e3bed4ed8c89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11538"/><div sID="gen20896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11538"/><hi type="bold">22. Sheba ... Raamah--</hi>in Arabia.<div eID="gen20896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief of ... spices--</hi>that is, best spices (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.15">De 33:15</reference>). Obtained from India and conveyed in caravans to Tyre. <div eID="gen20897" type="x-p"/>
entries.03b59a0233ed98f6f87147d59b2efaa93a112e6c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11539"/><div sID="gen20898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11539"/><hi type="bold">23. Haran--</hi>the dwelling-place of Abraham in Mesopotamia, after he moved from Ur (<reference osisRef="Gen.11.31">Ge 11:31</reference>).<div eID="gen20898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Canneh--</hi>Calneh, an Assyrian city on the Tigris; the Ctesiphon of the Greeks (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Ge 10:10</reference>).<div eID="gen20899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Eden--</hi>probably a region in Babylonia (see <reference osisRef="Gen.2.8">Ge 2:8</reference>).<div eID="gen20900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chilmad--</hi>a compound; the place designated by Ptolemy "Gaala of Media." The Chaldee version interprets it of Media. Henderson refers it to Carmanda, which Xenophon describes as a large city beyond the Euphrates. <div eID="gen20901" type="x-p"/>
entries.66ea09fdb2b48f0de19af20dd7ede3c47c334db6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11540"/><div sID="gen20902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11540"/><hi type="bold">24. all sorts of things--</hi>Hebrew, "perfections"; exquisite articles of finery [Grotius].<div eID="gen20902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clothes--</hi>rather, "mantles" or "cloaks"; literally, "wrappings." For "blue," Henderson translates, "purple."<div eID="gen20903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chests of rich apparel, bound with cords--</hi>treasures or repositories of damask stuffs, consisting of variegated threads woven together in figures [Henderson].<div eID="gen20904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cedar--</hi>The "chests" were made of cedar, in order to last the longer; and it also keeps off decay and has a sweet odor. <div eID="gen20905" type="x-p"/>
entries.14de9df7952c035afb6d224b569437b5b251d8fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11541"/><div sID="gen20906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11541"/><hi type="bold">25. sing of thee--</hi>personification; thy great merchant ships were palpable proofs of thy greatness. Others translate from a different Hebrew root, "were thy (mercantile) travellers." Fairbairn translates, "Were thy walls." But the parallelism to "thou wast glorious" favors English Version, "sing of thee." <div eID="gen20906" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1e0b893fe55b7e13ce443ca3138b93894805828: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11542"/><div sID="gen20907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11542"/>26. In contrast to her previous greatness, her downfall is here, by a sudden transition, depicted under the image of a vessel foundering at sea.<div eID="gen20907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">east wind--</hi>blowing from Lebanon, the most violent wind in the Mediterranean (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference>). A Levanter, as it is called. Nebuchadnezzar is meant. The "sea" is the war with him which the "rowers," or rulers of the state vessel, had "brought" it into, to its ruin. <div eID="gen20908" type="x-p"/>
entries.65fdb68fd19dccf5eadbd9fc581687dabe4615ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11543"/><div sID="gen20909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11543"/>27. The detailed enumeration implies the utter completeness of the ruin.<div eID="gen20909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and in all thy company--</hi>"even with all thy collected multitude" [Henderson]. <div eID="gen20910" type="x-p"/>
entries.c425a128e0ae3f07b2a14a7fa94b2eb5efff1721: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11544"/><div sID="gen20911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11544"/><hi type="bold">28. The suburbs--</hi>the buildings of Tyre on the adjoining continent. <div eID="gen20911" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebce17d39e05a9f8e033f00f4d9a60115f39f36e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11545"/><div sID="gen20912" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11545"/>29. So on the downfall of spiritual Babylon (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.17">Re 18:17</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen20912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20913" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall stand upon ... land--</hi>being cast out of their ships in which heretofore they prided themselves. <div eID="gen20913" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7db7dd582defc0e69b94b76bd121827f8bdb1aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11546"/><div sID="gen20914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11546"/><hi type="bold">30. against thee--</hi>rather, "concerning thee." <div eID="gen20914" type="x-p"/>
entries.024f3109c266b4f34bc909f47ccde2627eb57272: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11547"/><div sID="gen20915" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11547"/><hi type="bold">31. utterly bald--</hi>literally, "bald with baldness." The Phoenician custom in mourning; which, as being connected with heathenish superstitions, was forbidden to Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.14.1">De 14:1</reference>). <div eID="gen20915" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac6c36b8600ed6d353e7b185501e87fb00b2c71b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11548"/><div sID="gen20916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11548"/><hi type="bold">32. take up--</hi>lift up.<div eID="gen20916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the destroyed--</hi>a destroyed one. Literally, (as opposed to its previous bustle of thronging merchants and mariners, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.27">Eze 27:27</reference>), "one brought to death's stillness."<div eID="gen20917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in ... midst of ... sea--</hi>insular Tyre. <div eID="gen20918" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ee5c9ee70b9d51534848a704f576b93caa97547: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11549"/><div sID="gen20919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11549"/><hi type="bold">33. out of the seas--</hi>brought on shore out of the ships.<div eID="gen20919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">filledst--</hi>didst supply plentifully with wares.<div eID="gen20920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enrich ... kings--</hi>with the custom dues levied on the wares. <div eID="gen20921" type="x-p"/>

In the time when ... shall ... shall--</hi>Now that thou art broken (wrecked) ... thy merchandise ... are fallen [Maurer]. <div eID="gen20922" type="x-p"/>

entries.59ca1616b46fa35ffdb9801c9aa985410b1323bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11552"/><div sID="gen20924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11552"/><hi type="bold">36. hiss--</hi>with astonishment; as in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8">1Ki 9:8</reference>. <chapter eID="Ezek.27"/>

entries.d6f12d2431eec662493cbce7a130ef58da8f428c: <div eID="gen31988" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31990" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31989" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31991" type="x-p"/> This chapter may be considered as the second part of the prophecy concerning Tyre. The prophet pursues his subject in the manner of those ancient lamentations or funeral songs, in which the praeficiae or mourning women first recounted whatever was great or praiseworthy in the deceased, and then mourned his fall. Here the riches, glory, and extensive commerce of Tyre are enlarged upon, vv. 1-25. Her downfall is then described in a beautiful allegory, executed in a few words, with astonishing brevity, propriety, and perspicuity, <reference osisRef="Eze.27.26">Eze 27:26</reference>; upon which all the maritime and commercial world are represented as grieved and astonished at her fate, and greatly alarmed for their own, <reference osisRef="Eze.27.27-Eze.27.36">Eze 27:27-36</reference>. Besides the view which this chapter gives of the conduct of Providence, and the example with which it furnishes the critic and men of taste of a very elegant and highly finished piece of composition, it likewise affords the antiquary a very curious and interesting account of the wealth and commerce of ancient times. And to the mind that looks for "a city that hath foundations," what a picture does the whole present of the mutability and inanity of all earthly things! Many of the places mentioned in ancient history have, like Tyre, long ago lost their political consequence; the geographical situation of others cannot be traced; they have sunk in the deep waters of oblivion; the east wind hath carried them away.
entries.311788999f3369ed3f463824041223892cad4700: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31992" type="x-p"/> Take up a lamentation for Tyrus - This is a singular and curious chapter. It gives a very circumstantial account of the trade of Tyre with different parts of the world, and the different sorts of merchandise in which she trafficked. The places and the imports are as regularly entered here as they could have been in a European custom-house.
entries.67d42e055d49da3ab2ddbde9d0599768d93487ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31993" type="x-p"/> The entry of the sea - Tyre was a small island, or rather rock, in the sea, at a short distance from the main land. We have already seen that there was another Tyre on the main land; but they are both considered as one city.
entries.1daafaad704a2f3b695393b650b3c07986835cd8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31994" type="x-p"/> Thy builders have perfected thy beauty - Under the allegory of a beautiful ship, the prophet, here and in the following verses, paints the glory of this ancient city. Horace describes the commonwealth of Rome by the same allegory, and is as minute in his description, Carm. lib. 1. Od. xiv: - <div eID="gen31994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31995" type="x-p"/> O navis, referent in mare te novi <div eID="gen31995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31996" type="x-p"/> Fluctus? O quid agis? Fortiter occupa <div eID="gen31996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31997" type="x-p"/> Portum. Nonne video, ut <div eID="gen31997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31998" type="x-p"/> Nudum remigio latus, <div eID="gen31998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31999" type="x-p"/> Et malus celeri saucius Africo, <div eID="gen31999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32000" type="x-p"/> Antennaeque gemant? ac sine funibus <div eID="gen32000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32001" type="x-p"/> Vix durare carinae Possint imperiosius <div eID="gen32001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32002" type="x-p"/> Aequor! non tibi sunt integra lintea; <div eID="gen32002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32003" type="x-p"/> Non Di, quos iterum pressa votes malo: <div eID="gen32003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32004" type="x-p"/> Quamvis Pontica pinus, <div eID="gen32004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32005" type="x-p"/> Sylvae filia nobilis, <div eID="gen32005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32006" type="x-p"/> Jactes et genus, et nomen inutile <div eID="gen32006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32007" type="x-p"/> Nil pictis timidus navita puppibus <div eID="gen32007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32008" type="x-p"/> Fidit. Tu, nisi, ventis <div eID="gen32008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32009" type="x-p"/> Debes ludibrium, cave. <div eID="gen32009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32010" type="x-p"/> Unhappy vessel, shall the waves again <div eID="gen32010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32011" type="x-p"/> Tumultuous bear thee to the faithless main? <div eID="gen32011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32012" type="x-p"/> What, would thy madness thus with storms to sport? <div eID="gen32012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32013" type="x-p"/> Cast firm your anchor in the friendly port. <div eID="gen32013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32014" type="x-p"/> Behold thy naked decks, the wounded mast, <div eID="gen32014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32015" type="x-p"/> And sail-yards groan beneath the southern blast. <div eID="gen32015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32016" type="x-p"/> Nor, without ropes, thy keel can longer brave <div eID="gen32016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32017" type="x-p"/> The rushing fury of the imperious wave: <div eID="gen32017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32018" type="x-p"/> Torn are thy sails; thy guardian gods are lost, <div eID="gen32018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32019" type="x-p"/> Whom you might call, in future tempests tost. <div eID="gen32019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32020" type="x-p"/> What, though majestic in your pride you stood, <div eID="gen32020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32021" type="x-p"/> A noble daughter of the Pontic wood, <div eID="gen32021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32022" type="x-p"/> You now may vainly boast an empty name, <div eID="gen32022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32023" type="x-p"/> Of birth conspicuous in the rolls of fame. <div eID="gen32023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32024" type="x-p"/> The mariner, when storms around him rise, <div eID="gen32024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32025" type="x-p"/> No longer on a painted stern relies. <div eID="gen32025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32026" type="x-p"/> Ah! yet take heed, lest these new tempests sweep, <div eID="gen32026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32027" type="x-p"/> In sportive rage, thy glories to the deep. <div eID="gen32027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32028" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen32028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32029" type="x-p"/> I give this as a striking parallel to many passages in this chapter.
entries.0d0b35c6545237d0e9b1c3d59f0d68932af640bb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32030" type="x-p"/> Fir trees of Senir - Senir is a mountain which the Sidonians called Sirion, and the Hebrews Hermon, <reference osisRef="Deu.3.9">Deu 3:9</reference>. It was beyond Jordan, and extended from Libanus to the mountains of Gilead.
entries.233569f035ff5560ee197801970272f6f20cd5e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen32030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32031" type="x-p"/> Of the oaks of Bashan - Some translate alder, others the pine. <div eID="gen32031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32032" type="x-p"/> The company of the Ashurites - The word אשרים asherim is by several translated boxwood. The seats or benches being made of this wood inlaid with ivory. <div eID="gen32032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32033" type="x-p"/> Isles of Chittim - The Italian islands; the islands of Greece; Cyprus. Calmet says Macedonia is meant.
entries.96b6a83f79cdbcaacdc8e67878d11f30598dd6ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32034" type="x-p"/> Fine linen - שש shesh, cotton cloth. In this sense the word is generally to be understood. <div eID="gen32034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32035" type="x-p"/> To be thy sail - Probably the flag - ensign or pennant, is meant. <div eID="gen32035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32036" type="x-p"/> Blue and purple from the isles of Elishah - Elis, a part of the Peloponnesus.
entries.18ab3f6f60cadb73067f9214fba524cdb40cd0df: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen32036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32037" type="x-p"/> Zidon and Arvad - Or Arad. Two powerful cities on the Phoenician coast, in the neighborhood of Tyre, from which Tyre had her sailors; and the best instructed of her own inhabitants were her pilots or steersmen.
entries.89bf0157517843a44f049bcb897d84263e854a62: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32038" type="x-p"/> The ancients of Gebal - This was a city of Phoenicia, near Mount Libanus, <reference osisRef="Jos.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>. It was called Biblos by the Greeks. <div eID="gen32038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32039" type="x-p"/> Thy calkers - Those who repaired their vessels; paying, as it is termed, pitched hemp into the seams, to prevent the water from oozing through. <div eID="gen32039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32040" type="x-p"/> To occupy thy merchandise - That is, to be thy agents or factors.
entries.360380c3920a9af0c844d76284aa693c1ee146ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32041" type="x-p"/> They of Persia - Lud, the Lydians; Phut, a people of Africa, see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen 10:6</reference>. From these places they had auxiliary troops; for as they traded with the then known world, were rich, and could afford to give good pay, they no doubt had soldiers and sailors from every part. Skilful and desperate men will go any where after their price.
entries.409372140bba170429a0eff2732beb1235f2d26a: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen32041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32042" type="x-p"/> The Gammadims were in thy towers - Some think these were a people of Phoenicia; others, that tutelar images are meant; others, that the word expresses strong men, Who acted as guards. The Vulgate reads Pygmaei, the pygmies, who were fabled to be a little people of a cubit in height, from גמד gomed. a cubit; and are told that this little people were celebrated for their wars with the cranes; but nothing of this kind can enter into this description. Probably a people inhabiting the promontories of Phoenicia are here intended; and their hanging their shields upon the walls is a proof that soldiers are meant, and persons of skill and prowess too.
entries.18afbcaa7460122479ab6b2b4180e675c43d794d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32043" type="x-p"/> Tarshish was thy merchant - After having given an account of the naval and military equipment of this city, he now speaks of the various places and peoples with whom the Tyrians traded, and the different kinds of merchandise imported from those places. <div eID="gen32043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32044" type="x-p"/> By Tarshish some understand the Carthaginians; some think Tartessus, near the straits of Gibraltar, is meant; others, Tharsis in Cilicia. The place was famous for all the useful metals, silver, iron, tin, and lead. All these they might have had from Britain.
entries.4ac9bd3dda714314fa5c0eb9838a1d0e110ba129: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32045" type="x-p"/> Javan, Tubal, and Meshech - The Ionians, the Tybarenians, and the Cappadocians, or Muscovites. <div eID="gen32045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32046" type="x-p"/> They traded the persons of men - That is, they trafficked in slaves. The bodies and souls of men were bought and sold in those days, as in our degenerate age. With these also they traded in brazen vessels.
entries.35514ff92eabd592fb48aeff78ce7977389e3db4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen32046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32047" type="x-p"/> Togarmah - The Sarmatians. Some think Cappadocia. With these they dealt in horses, mules, and horsemen; or probably draught horses and war horses are intended.
entries.7ece72318769d363916b1c6e02f474bc170b65fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32048" type="x-p"/> The men of Dedan - Dedan was one of the descendants of Abraham by Keturah, and dwelt in Arabia, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.3">Gen 25:3</reference>. Ivory and ebony might come from that quarter. By way of distinction ivory is called both in Hebrew ש shen, and in Arabic shen, the Tooth, as that beautiful substance is the tooth of the elephant.
entries.de0e26323a5ca1a7be07dcdd1f9a6d936a4bc04c: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32049" type="x-p"/> Syria - These were always a mercantile people. For the precious stones mentioned here see the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.28.17">Exo 28:17</reference> (note).
entries.cefe75a01f6614960303d0ae0d901b6afcedf609: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32050" type="x-p"/> Judah, and the land of Israel - traded in thy market wheat - The words have been understood as articles of merchandise, not names of places. So the Jews traded with the Tyrians in wheat, stacte, balsam, honey, oil, and resin.
entries.703da89edd1e5dac27e7a8baccfdbe6bb6bcbb92: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32051" type="x-p"/> Damascus wine of Helbon - Now called by the Turks Haleb, and by us Aleppo. <div eID="gen32051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32052" type="x-p"/> White wool - Very fine wool: wool of a fine quality. Some think Milesian wool is meant.
entries.49e56bcf1022e2470c21198838999dabb0850bc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32053" type="x-p"/> Dan also and Javan - It is probable that both these words mean some of the Grecian islands. <div eID="gen32053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32054" type="x-p"/> Going to and fro - They both took and brought - imported and exported: but מאוזל meuzal, from uzal, may be a proper name. What place is signified I cannot tell, unless it be Azal, a name, according to Kamoos, of the capital of Arabia Felix.
entries.509236730ad7eab8db6cbf7d8eb201a1faf4ee91: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32055" type="x-p"/> Dedan - Possibly the descendants of Dedan, son of Raamah, see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference>. <div eID="gen32055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32056" type="x-p"/> In precious clothes for chariots - Either fine carpets, or rich housings for horses, camels, etc., used for riding.
entries.caaee413cd9eff4b38267ca5652cd287b7f8acac: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32057" type="x-p"/> Arabia, and all the princes of Cedar - Arabia Deserta, on the confines of the Dead Sea. The Kedarenes inhabited the same country. <div eID="gen32057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32058" type="x-p"/> These brought lambs, rams, and goats for the consumption of the city.
entries.26c11d07f260cb78cb52e4a240dabf33c8fea9ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen32058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32059" type="x-p"/> Sheba and Raamah - Inhabitants of Arabia Felix, at the entrance of the Persian Gulf, who were famous for their riches and spices.
entries.8424cb8c8ffc7faf560b7ab1c94753213cbd02b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen32059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32060" type="x-p"/> Haran - In Mesopotamia; well known in Scripture. <div eID="gen32060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32061" type="x-p"/> Canneh - Or Chalane, see <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>. It is supposed to be a cape or port of Arabia Felix, on the Indian Sea. <div eID="gen32061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32062" type="x-p"/> Eden - Equally famous: supposed to have been situated near the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates. <div eID="gen32062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32063" type="x-p"/> Sheba - Different from that in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Gen 10:22</reference>. This was probably near the country of the Edomites. <div eID="gen32063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32064" type="x-p"/> Asshur - Perhaps the Assyrians. <div eID="gen32064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32065" type="x-p"/> Chilmad - Possibly Cholmadora, on the Euphrates. Ptol. lib. v.. cap. 15. For several of these places, and the persons from whom they derived their names, see Genesis 10 (note), and the notes there; and see Calmet.
entries.697398d59bc1974313260a3b3bb2e69ce1a55079: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen32065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32066" type="x-p"/> These were thy merchants in all sorts of things - The above people traded with the Tyrians in a great variety of the most valuable merchandise: blue or purple cloth, boxes of cedar, covered with skins, and bound with silken cords, and sealed with an engraved seal, finely cut, etc. See the Chaldee.
entries.f14e501840a92d5f25e507387ad49ce1fbbe89e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen32066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32067" type="x-p"/> The ships of Tarshish - The ships of Tharsis, in Cilicia, were the chief of those which traded with thee.
entries.e28e7b81f3d8348ec7f31263ff3ffabea3345a0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen32067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32068" type="x-p"/> Thy rowers have brought thee into great waters - Tyre is still considered under the allegory of a ship; and all the vessels of different nations trading with her are represented as towing her into deep waters - bringing her into great affluence. But while in this state, a stormy east wind, or a destructive wind, meaning the Chaldeans, arises, and dashes her to pieces! See the ode from Horace, already quoted on <reference osisRef="Eze.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference> (note).
entries.c05c4326ab57da194860294ae23e05e27b80e607: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen32068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32069" type="x-p"/> Thy riches - This vast ship, laden with all kinds of valuable wares, and manned in the best manner, being wrecked, all her valuables, sailors, officers, etc., went to the bottom.
entries.85b53c304af8c26f21e73cadb39e76978439ffd8: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen32069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32070" type="x-p"/> The cry of thy pilots - When the ship was dashed against the rocks by the violence of the winds and the waves, and all hope of life was taken away, then a universal cry was set up by all on board. I have heard this cry, and nothing more dismal can be imagined, when the ship by a violent tempest is driving among rocks on a lee shore. Then "All lost! cut away the boat!" is more dreadful than the cry of fire at midnight.
