entries.f8d08b5cfa819e9c5e4f2ee046529e55e9a8837e: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen32070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32071" type="x-p"/> Shall cry bitterly - All that were on the land, seeing this dreadful sight, a gallant ship perishing with all her men and goods, are represented as setting up a dismal cry at this heart-rending sight. But what must they have felt who were on board? Reader, wert thou ever shipwrecked? Wert thou ever in a hurricane on a lee rocky shore, where the helm had lost its power, and the sails were rendered useless? Dost thou remember that apparently last moment, when the ship drove up to the tremendous rocks, riding on the back of a mountainous surge? Then what was the universal cry? Hast thou ever heard any thing so terrific? so appalling? so death and judgment-like? No. It is impossible. These are the circumstances, this is the cry, that the prophet describes; disorder, confusion, dismay, and ruin. And this is a scene which the present writer has witnessed, himself a part of the wretched, when all hope of life was taken away, the yawning gulf opened, and nothing presented itself to support body or soul but that God who gave to both their being, and ultimately rescued him and his forlorn companions from one of the worst of deaths, by heaving the ship from the rocks by the agency of a tremendous receding wave. My soul hath these things still in remembrance, and therefore is humbled within me.
entries.6306f798103b95ce05e401c18c298cf7013d5c54: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen32071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32072" type="x-p"/> What city is like Tyrus - This, to the end of the chapter, is the lamentation.
entries.97f158c7555e0c34461f099c837dbcbeffd8eee4: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen32072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32073" type="x-p"/> Shall hiss at thee - שרקו shareku, shall shriek for thee. This powerfully expresses the sensation made on the feelings of the spectators on the shore when they saw the vessel swallowed up.  <chapter eID="Ezek.27"/> <div eID="gen32073" type="x-p"/>

entries.9be01c53e85876aa4309cc745613f4b6b0ce1beb: <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.1-Ezek.27.11">Eze 27:1-11</reference> <div eID="gen15041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> The lamentation commences with a picture of the glory of the city of Tyre, its situation, its architectural beauty, its military strength and defences (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3-Ezek.27.11">Eze 27:3-11</reference>), and its wide-spread commercial relations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12-Ezek.27.25">Eze 27:12-25</reference>); and then passes into mournful lamentation over the ruin of all this glory (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26-Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:26-36</reference>). <div eID="gen15042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15043" type="x-p"/> Introduction and description of the glory and might of Tyre. - Eze 27:1. <hi type="italic">And the word of Jehovah came to me, saying,</hi> Eze 27:2. <hi type="italic">And do thou, O son of man, raise a lamentation over Tyre,</hi> Eze 27:3. <hi type="italic">And say to Tyre, Thou who dwellest at the approaches of the sea, merchant of the nations to many islands, thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Tyre, thou sayest, I am perfect in beauty.</hi> Eze 27:4. <hi type="italic">In the heart of the seas is thy territory; thy builders have made thy beauty perfect.</hi> Eze 27:5. <hi type="italic">Out of cypresses of Senir they built all double-plank-work for thee; they took cedars of Lebanon to make a mast upon thee.</hi> Eze 27:6. <hi type="italic">They made thine oars of oaks of Bashan, thy benches they made of ivory set in box from the islands of the Chittaeans.</hi> Eze 27:7. <hi type="italic">Byssus in embroidery from Egypt was thy sail, to serve thee for a banner; blue and red purple from the islands of Elishah was thine awning.</hi> Eze 27:8. <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Sidon and Arvad were thy rowers; thy skilful men, O Tyre, were in thee, they were thy sailors.</hi> Eze 27:9. <hi type="italic">The elders of Gebal and its skilful men were with thee to repair thy leaks; all the ships of the sea and their mariners were in thee to barter thy goods.</hi> Eze 27:10. <hi type="italic">Persian and Lydian and Libyan were in thine army, thy men of war; shield and helmet they hung up in thee; they gave brilliancy to thee.</hi> Eze 27:11. <hi type="italic">The sons of Arvad and thine army were upon thy walls round about, and brave men were upon they towers; they hung up their shields upon thy walls round about; they have made thy beauty perfect.</hi> - The lamentation commences with an address to Tyre, in which its favourable situation for purposes of trade, and the perfect beauty of which she was conscious, are placed in the foreground (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.3">Eze 27:3</reference>). Tyre is sitting, or dwelling, at the approaches of the sea. מבואת ים, approaches or entrances of the sea, are harbours into which ships sail and from which they depart, just as מבוא העיר sa t, the gate of the city, it both entrance and exit. This description does not point to the city on the mainland, or Old Tyre, but answers exactly to Insular Tyre with its two harbours.<note placement="foot">Insular Tyre possessed two harbours, a northern one called the Sidonian, because it was on the Sidonian side, and one on the opposite or south-eastern side, which was called the Egyptian harbour from the direction in which it pointed. The Sidonian was the more celebrated of the two, and consisted of an inner harbour, situated within the wall of the city, and an outer one, formed by a row of rocks, which lay at a distance of about three hundred paces to the north-west of the island, and ran parallel to the opposite coast of the mainland, so as to form a roadstead in which ships could anchor (vid., Arrian, ii. 20; Strabo, xvi. 2. 23). This northern harbour is still held by the city of <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>, whereas the Egyptian harbour with the south-eastern portion of the island has been buried by the sand driven against the coasts by the south winds, so that even the writers of the Middle Ages make no allusion to it. (See Movers, <hi type="italic">Phönizier</hi>, II. 1, pp. 214ff.).</note> ישׁבתי, with the connecting <hi type="italic">i</hi>, which is apparently confounded here after the Aramaean fashion with the <hi type="italic">i</hi> of the feminine pronoun, and has therefore been marked by the Masora as superfluous (vid., Ewald, §211 <hi type="italic">b</hi>). The combination of רכלת with 'אל איּים ר may be accounted for from the primary meaning of רכל, to travel about as a merchant: thou who didst go to the nations on many shores to carry on thy trade. Tyre itself considers that she is perfect in her beauty, partly on account of her strong position in the sea, and partly because of her splendid edifices.<note placement="foot">Curtius, iv. 2: <hi type="italic">Tyrus et claritate et magnitudine ante omnes urbes Syriae Phoenicesque memorabilis.</hi> (Cf. Strabo, xvi. 2. 22.)</note> <div eID="gen15043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> In the description which follows of this beauty and glory, from <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference> onwards, Tyre is depicted allegorically as a beautiful ship, splendidly built and equipped throughout, and its destruction is afterwards represented as a shipwreck occasioned by the east wind (Eze 27:26.).<note placement="foot">Jerome recognised this allegory, and has explained it correctly as follows: “He (the prophet) speaks τροπικῶς, as though addressing a ship, and points out its beauty and the abundance of everything. Then, after having depicted all its supplies, he announces that a storm will rise, and the south wind (<hi type="italic">auster</hi>) will blow, by which great waves will be gathered up, and the vessel will be wrecked. In all this he is referring to the overthrow of the city by King Nabuchodonosor,” etc. Rashi and others give the same explanation.</note> <div eID="gen15044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15045" type="x-p"/> The words, “in the heart of the seas is thy territory” (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference></hi>), are equally applicable to the city of Tyre and to a ship, the building of which is described in what follows. The comparison of Tyre to a ship was very naturally suggested by the situation of the city in the midst of the sea, completely surrounded by water. As a ship, it must of necessity be built of wood. The shipbuilders selected the finest kinds of wood for the purpose; cypresses of Antilibanus for double planks, which formed the sides of the vessel, and cedar of Lebanon for the mast. <hi type="italic">Senir</hi>, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">Deu 3:9</reference>, was the Amoritish name of <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi> or <hi type="italic">Antilibanus</hi>, whereas the Sidonians called it <hi type="italic">Sirion</hi>. On the other hand, <hi type="italic">Senir</hi> occurs in <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.23">1Ch 5:23</reference>, and Sh<hi type="italic">e</hi>nir in Sol 4:8, in connection with <hi type="italic">Hermon</hi>, where they are used to denote separate portions of Antilibanus. Ezekiel evidently uses <hi type="italic">Senir</hi> as a foreign name, which had been retained to his own time, whereas <hi type="italic">Sirion</hi> had possibly become obsolete, as the names had both the same meaning (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">Deu 3:9</reference>). The naming of the places from which the several materials were obtained for the fitting out of the ship, serve to heighten the glory of its construction and give an ideal character to the picture. All lands have contributed their productions to complete the glory and might of Tyre. Cypress-wood was frequently used by the ancients for buildings and (according to Virgil, <hi type="italic">Georg</hi>. ii. 443) also for ships, because it was exempt from the attacks of worms, and was almost imperishable, and yet very light (<hi type="italic">Theophr. Hist.</hi> plant. v. 8; Plinii <hi type="italic">Hist. nat.</hi> xvi. 79). לחתים, a dual form, like חמתים in 2Ki 25:4; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>, double-planks, used for the two side-walls of the ship. For oars they chose oaks of Bashan (משּׁוט as well as משׁוט in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.29">Eze 27:29</reference> from שׁוּט, to row), and the rowing benches (or deck) were of ivory inlaid in box. קרשׁ is used in Exo 26:15. for the boards or planks of the wooden walls of the tabernacle; here it is employed in a collective sense, either for the rowing benches, of which there were at least two, and sometimes three rows in a vessel, one above another, or more properly, for the deck of the vessel (Hitzig). This was made of she4n, or ivory, inlaid in wood. The ivory is mentioned first as the most valuable material of the קרשׁ, the object being to picture the ship as possessing all possible splendour. The expression בּתּ־אשּׁרים, occasions some difficulty, partly on account of the use of the word בּת, and partly in connection with the meaning of  אשּׁרים , although so much may be inferred from the context, that the allusion is to some kind of wood inlaid with ivory, and the custom of inlaying wood with ivory for the purpose of decoration is attested by Virgil, <hi type="italic">Aen</hi>. x. 137:<hi type="italic">“Vel quale per artem Inclusum buxo, aut Oricia terebintho Lucet ebur.”</hi> <div eID="gen15045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> But the use of בּת does not harmonize with the relation of the wood to the ivory inserted in wood; nor can it be defended by the fact that in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.3">Lam 3:3</reference> an arrow is designated “the son of the quiver.” According to this analogy, the ivory ought to have been called the son of the Ashurim, because the ivory is inserted in the wood, and not the wood in the ivory.<note placement="foot">The Targum has paraphrased it in this way: דפּין דאשׁכרעין מכבשׁין בשׁן דפיל, i.e., planks of box or pine inlaid with ivory.</note> <div eID="gen15046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> We must therefore adopt the solution proposed by R. Salomo and others - namely, that the Masoretic division of בת־אשּׁרים into two words is founded upon a mistake, and that it should be read as one word בּתאשּׁרים, ivory in תּאשּׁרים, i.e., either sherbin-cedar (according to more recent expositors), or box-wood, for which Bochart (<hi type="italic">Phal</hi>. III 5) has decided. The fact that in <reference osisRef="Isa.60.13">Isa 60:13</reference> the תּאשּׁוּר is mentioned among the trees growing upon Lebanon, whereas here the תּאשּׁרים are described as coming from the islands of the כּתּיּם, does not furnish a decisive argument to the contrary. We cannot determine with certainty what species of tree is referred to, and therefore it cannot be affirmed that the tree grew upon Lebanon alone, and not upon the islands of the Mediterranean. כּתּיּם are the Κιτιεῖς, the inhabitants of the port of Κίτιον in Cyprus; then the Cyprians generally; and here, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.10">Jer 2:10</reference>, where איּים of the כּתּיּם are mentioned, in a still broader sense, inhabitants of Cyprus and other islands and coast-lands of the Mediterranean. In 1 Macc. 1:1 and 8:5, even Macedonia is reckoned as belonging to the γὴ Χεττειεῖμ or Κιτίεων. Consequently the place from which the תּאשּׁרים were brought does not furnish any conclusive proof that the Cyprian pine is referred to, although this was frequently used for ship-building. There is just as much ground for thinking of the box, as Bochart does, and we may appeal in support of this to the fact that, according to Theophrastus, there is no place in which it grows more vigorously than on the island of Corsica. In any case, Ezekiel mentions it as a very valuable kind of wood; though we cannot determine with certainty to what wood he refers, either from the place where it grew or from the accounts of the ancients concerning the kinds of wood that ship-builders used. The reason for this, however, is a very simple one - namely, that the whole description has an ideal character, and, as Hitzig has correctly observed, “the application of the several kinds of wood to the different parts of the ship is evidently only poetical.” <div eID="gen15047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15048" type="x-p"/> The same may be said of the materials of which, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.7">Eze 27:7</reference>, the sails and awning of the ship were made. <hi type="italic">Byssus</hi> in party-coloured work (רקמה, see comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.26.36">Exo 26:36</reference>), i.e., woven in mixed colours, probably not merely in stripes, but woven with figures and flowers.”<note placement="foot">See Wilkinson, <hi type="italic">Manners and Customs</hi>, III Pl. xvi., where engravings are given of Egyptian state-ships with embroidered sails. On one ship a large square sail is displayed in purple-red and purple-blue checks, surrounded by a gold border. The vessel of Antony and Cleopatra in the battle of Actium had also purple sails; and in this case the purple sails were the sign of the admiral’s ship, just as in Ezekiel they serve as a mark of distinction (נס). See Movers, II 3, p. 165, where the accounts of ancient writers concerning such state-ships are collected together.</note> “From Egypt;” the byssus-weaving of Egypt was celebrated in antiquity, so that byssus-linen formed one of the principal articles of export (vid., Movers, <hi type="italic">ut supra</hi>, pp. 317ff.). מפרשׁ, literally, spreading out, evidently signifies the sail, which we expect to find mentioned here, and with which the following clause, “to serve thee for a banner,” can be reconciled, inasmuch as it may be assumed either that the sails also served for a banner, because the ships had no actual flag, like those in Wilkinson’s engraving, or that the flag (נס) being also extended is included under the term מפרשׁ (Hitzig). The covering of the ship, i.e., the awning which was put up above the deck for protection from the heat of the sun, consisted of purple (תכלת and ארגּמן, see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.25.4">Exo 25:4</reference>) from the islands of <hi type="italic">Elishah</hi>, i.e., of the Grecian Peloponesus, which naturally suggests the Laconian purple so highly valued in antiquity on account of its splendid colour (Plin. <hi type="italic">Hist. nat.</hi> ix. 36, xxi. 8). The account of the building of the ship is followed by the manning, and the attention paid to its condition. The words of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.8">Eze 27:8</reference></hi> may be taken as referring quite as much to the ship as to the city, which was in possession of ships, and is mentioned by name in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.8">Eze 27:8</reference></hi>. The reference to the <hi type="italic">Sidonians</hi> and <hi type="italic">Arvad</hi>, i.e., to the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Aradus</hi>, a rocky island to the north of Tripolis, as rowers, is not at variance with the latter; since there is no need to understand by the rowers either slaves or servants employed to row, and the Tyrians certainly drew their rowers from the whole of the Phoenician population, whereas the chief men in command of the ships, the captain and pilot (חבלים), were no doubt as a rule citizens of Tyre. The introduction of the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Gebal</hi>, i.e., the <hi type="italic">Byblos</hi> of the Greeks, the present <hi type="italic">Jebail</hi>, between Tripolis and Berytus (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Josh.13.5">Jos 13:5</reference>), who were noted even in Solomon’s time as skilful architects (1 Kings 5:32), as repairers of the leak, decidedly favours the supposition that the idea of the ship is still kept in the foreground; and by the naming of those who took charge of the piloting and condition of the vessel, the thought is expressed that all the cities of Phoenicia assisted to maintain the might and glory of Tyre, since Tyre was supreme in Phoenicia. It is not till <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.9">Eze 27:9</reference></hi> that the allegory falls into the background. Tyre now appears no longer as a ship, but as a maritime city, into which all the ships of the sea sail, to carry on and improve her commerce. <div eID="gen15048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">Eze 27:10</reference>, Eze 27:11. Tyre had also made the best provision for its defence. It maintained an army of mercenary troops from foreign countries to protect its colonies and extend its settlements, and entrusted the guarding of the walls of the city to fighting men of Phoenicia. The hired troops specially named in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.10">Eze 27:10</reference> are <hi type="italic">Pharas</hi>, <hi type="italic">Lud</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Phut</hi>. פּוּט is no doubt an African tribe, in Coptic <hi type="italic">Phaiat</hi>, the Libyans of the ancients, who had spread themselves over the whole of North Africa as far as Mauretania (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.6">Gen 10:6</reference>). לוּד is not the Semitic people of that name, the Lydians (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.22">Gen 10:22</reference>), but here, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Isa 66:19</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>, the Hamitic people of לוּדים (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.13">Gen 10:13</reference>), probably a general name for the whole of the Moorish tribes, since לוּד (<reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>) and לוּדים (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.9">Jer 44:9</reference>) are mentioned in connection with פּוּט as auxiliaries in the Egyptian army. There is something striking in the reference to פּרס, the Persians. Hävernick points to the early intercourse carried on by the Phoenicians with Persia through the Persian Gulf, through which the former would not doubt be able to obtain mercenary soldiers, for which it was a general rule to select tribes as remote as possible. Hitzig objects to this, on the ground that there is no proof that this intercourse with Persian through the Persian Gulf was carried on in Ezekiel’s time, and that even if it were, it does not follow that there were any Persian mercenaries. He therefore proposes to understand by פרס, Persians who had settled in Africa in the olden time. But this settlement cannot be inferred with sufficient certainty either from Sallust, <hi type="italic">Jug</hi>. c. 18, or from the occurrence of the African Μάκαι of Herodotus, iv. 175, along with the Asiatic (Ptol. vi. 7. 14), to take it as an explanation of פּרס. If we compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.38.5">Eze 38:5</reference>, where <hi type="italic">Pâras</hi>is mentioned in connection with <hi type="italic">Cush</hi> and <hi type="italic">Phut</hi>, <hi type="italic">Gomer</hi> and <hi type="italic">Togarmah</hi>, as auxiliaries in the army of <hi type="italic">Gog</hi>, there can be no doubt that Asiatic Persians are intended there. And we have to take the word in the same sense here; for Hitzig’s objections consist of pure conjectures which have no conclusive force. Ezekiel evidently intends to give the names of tribes from the far-off east, west, and south, who were enlisted as mercenaries in the military service of Tyre. Hanging the shields and helmets in the city, to ornament its walls, appears to have been a Phoenician custom, which Solomon also introduced into Judah (1Ki 10:16-17, Sol 4:4), and which is mentioned again in the times of the Maccabees (1 Macc. 4:57). - A distinction is drawn in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.11">Eze 27:11</reference> between the mercenary troops on the one hand, and the Aradians, and הילך, thine army, the military corps consisting of Tyrians, on the other. The latter appears upon the walls of Tyre, because native troops were employed to watch and defend the city, whilst the mercenaries had to march into the field. The ἁπ. λεγ. גּמּדים (<hi type="italic">Gammâdim</hi>) signifies brave men, as Roediger has conclusively shown from the Syrian usage, in his <hi type="italic">Addenda</hi> to Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 70f. It is therefore an <hi type="italic">epitheton</hi> of the native troops of Tyre. - With the words, “they (the troops) completed thy beauty,” the picture of the glory of Tyre is rounded off, returning to its starting-point in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference> and Eze 27:5.
entries.a47470005c3dec2445625b137d15887d78a2130b: <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12-Ezek.27.25">Eze 27:12-25</reference> <div eID="gen15049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> This is followed by a description of the commerce of Tyre with all nations, who delivered their productions in the market of this metropolis of the commerce of the world, and received the wares and manufactures of this city in return. - Eze 27:12. <hi type="italic">Tarshish traded with thee for the multitude of goods of all kinds; with silver, iron, tin, and lead they paid for thy sales.</hi> Eze 27:13. <hi type="italic">Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants; with souls of men and brazen vessels they made thy barter.</hi> Eze 27:14. <hi type="italic">From the house of Togarmah they paid horses, riding-horses, and mules for thy sales.</hi> Eze 27:15. <hi type="italic">The sons of Dedan were thy merchants; many islands were at thy hand for commerce; ivory horns and ebony they brought thee in payment.</hi> Eze 27:16. <hi type="italic">Aram traded with thee for the multitude of thy productions; with carbuncle, red purple, and embroidery, and byssus, and corals, and rubies they paid for thy sales.</hi> Eze 27:17. <hi type="italic">Judah and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants; with wheat of Minnith and confectionery, and honey and oil, and balsam they made thy barter.</hi> Eze 27:18. <hi type="italic">Damascus traded with thee in the multitude of thy productions, for the multitude of goods of all kinds, with wine of Chelbon and white wool.</hi> Eze 27:19. <hi type="italic">Vedan and Javan from Uzal gave wrought iron for thy salves; cassia and calamus were for thy barter.</hi> Eze 27:20. <hi type="italic">Vedan was thy merchant in cloths spread for riding. Eze 27:21. Arabia and all the princes of Kedar, they were at thy hand for commerce; lambs and rams and he-goats, in these they traded with thee.</hi> Eze 27:22. <hi type="italic">The merchants of Sheba and Ragmah, they were thy merchants; with all kinds of costly spices and with all kinds of precious stones and gold they paid for thy sales.</hi> Eze 27:23. <hi type="italic">Haran, and Canneh, and Eden, the merchants of Sheba, Asshur, Chilmad, were they merchants;</hi> Eze 27:24. <hi type="italic">They were thy merchants in splendid clothes, in purple and embroidered robes, and in treasures of twisted yarn, in wound and strong cords for thy wares.</hi> Eze 27:25. <hi type="italic">The ships of Tarshish were thy caravans, thy trade, and thou wast filled and glorious in the heart of the seas.</hi> - The enumeration of the different peoples, lands, and cities, which carried on trade with Tyre, commences with Tarshish (Tartessus) in the extreme west, then turns to the north, passes through the different lands of Anterior Asia and the Mediterranean to the remotest north-east, and ends by mentioning Tarshish again, to round off the list. But the lands and peoples, which are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.5-Ezek.27.11">Eze 27:5-11</reference> as furnishing produce and manufactures for the building of Tyre, viz., Egypt and the tribes of Northern Africa, are left out. - To avoid wearisome uniformity in the enumeration, Ezekiel has used interchangeably the synonymous words which the language possessed for trade, besides endeavouring to give life to the description by a variety of turns of expression. Thus סחרתך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12">Eze 27:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">Eze 27:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.18">Eze 27:18</reference>), סחריך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.21">Eze 27:21</reference>), and סחרת ידך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference>), or סחרי ידך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.21">Eze 27:21</reference>), are interchanged with רכליך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.13">Eze 27:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.22">Eze 27:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.24">Eze 27:24</reference>), רכלתך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">Eze 27:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.23">Eze 27:23</reference>), and מרכּלתּך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.24">Eze 27:24</reference>); and, again, נתן עזבוניך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12">Eze 27:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.14">Eze 27:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.22">Eze 27:22</reference>), נתן  (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">Eze 27:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.19">Eze 27:19</reference>), with נתן מערבך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.13">Eze 27:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>), and בּמערבך היה (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.19">Eze 27:19</reference>), and השׁיב אשׁכּרך (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference>). The words סחר, participle of סחר, and רכל, from רכל morf, signify merchants, traders, who travel through different lands for purposes of trade. סחרת, literally, the female trader; and סחרה, literally, trade; then used as abstract for concrete, the tradesman or merchant. רכל, the travelling merchant. -  רכלת, the female trader, a city carrying on trade. מרכלת, trade or a place of trade, a commercial town. עזבונים (<hi type="italic">pluralet</hi>.) does not mean a place of trade, market, and profits (Gesenius and others); but according to its derivation from עזב, to leave, relinquish, literally, leaving or giving up, and as Gusset. has correctly explained it, “that which you leave with another in the place of something else which he has given up to you.” Ewald, in accordance with this explanation, has adopted the very appropriate rendering <hi type="italic">Absatz</hi>, or sale. נתן עזבוניך, with ב, or with a double accusative, literally, to make thy sale with something, i.e., to pay or to give, i.e., pay, something as an equivalent for the sale; 'נתן בּעזב, to give something for the sale, or the goods to be sold. מערב, barter, goods bartered with נתן, to give bartered goods, or carry on trade by barter. <div eID="gen15050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> The following are the countries and peoples enumerated: - תּרשׁישׁ, the Tyrian colony of <hi type="italic">Tarshish</hi> or <hi type="italic">Tartessus</hi>, in <hi type="italic">Hispania Baetica</hi>, which was celebrated for its wealth in silver (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.9">Jer 10:9</reference>), and, according to the passage before us, also supplied iron, tin, and lead (vid., Plin. <hi type="italic">Hist. nat</hi>. iii. 3 4, xxxiii. 6 31, xxiv. 14 41; Diod. Sic. v. 38). Further particulars concerning Tarshish are to be found in Movers, <hi type="italic">Phoeniz</hi>. II 2, pp. 588ff., and II 3, p. 36. - <hi type="italic">Javan</hi>, i.e., Jania, Greece or Greeks. - <hi type="italic">Tubal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Meshech</hi> are the <hi type="italic">Tibareni</hi> and <hi type="italic">Moschi</hi> of the ancients between the Black and Caspian Seas (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.2">Gen 10:2</reference>). They supplied souls of men, i.e., slaves, and things in brass. The slave trade was carried on most vigorously by the Ionians and Greeks (see Joel 4:6, from which we learn that the Phoenicians sold prisoners of war to them); and both Greeks and Romans drew their largest supplies and the best slaves from the Pontus (for proofs of this, see Movers, II 3, pp. 81f.). It is probable that the principal supplies of brazen articles were furnished by the Tibareni and Moschi, as the Colchian mountains still contain an inexhaustible quantity of copper. In Greece, copper was found and wrought in <hi type="italic">Euboea</hi> alone; and the only other rich mines were in Cyprus (vid., Movers, II 3, pp. 66, 67). - Eze 27:14. “From the house of <hi type="italic">Togarmah</hi> they paid,” i.e., they of the house of Togarmah paid. <hi type="italic">Togarmah</hi> is one of the names of the <hi type="italic">Armenians</hi> (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.3">Gen 10:3</reference>); and Strabo (XI 14. 9) mentions the wealth of Armenia in horses, whilst that in asses is attested by Herodotus (i. 194), so that we may safely infer that mules were also bred there. - Eze 27:15. The sons of <hi type="italic">Dedan</hi>, or the Dedanites, are, no doubt, the Dedanites mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference> as descendants of Cush, who conducted the carrying trade between the Persian Gulf and Tyre, and whose caravans are mentioned in Isa 21:13. Their relation to the Semitic Dedanites, who are evidently intended in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">Eze 27:20</reference>, and by the inhabitants of <hi type="italic">Dedan</hi> mentioned in connection with Edom in <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.13">Eze 25:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.49.8">Jer 49:8</reference>, is involved in obscurity (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference>). The combination with איּים רבּים and the articles of commerce which they brought to Tyre, point to a people of southern Arabia settled in the neighbourhood of the Persian Gulf. The many איּים are the islands and coasts of Arabia on the Persian Gulf and Erythraean Sea.<note placement="foot">Movers (II 3, pp. 303ff.) adduces still further evidence in addition to that given above, namely, that “unquestionable traces of the ancient name have been preserved in the region in which the ancient Dedanites are represented as living, partly on the coast in the names <hi type="italic">Attana, Attene</hi>, which have been modified according to well-known laws, - the former, a commercial town on the Persian Gulf, visited by Roman merchants (Plin. vi. 32, §147); the latter, a tract of country opposite to the island of Tylos (Plin. <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> §49), - and partly in the islands of the Persian Gulf” (p. 304).</note> סחרת ידך, the commerce of thy hand, i.e., as <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concr</hi>., those who were ready to thy hand as merchants. קרנות שׁן, ivory horns. This is the term applied to the elephants’ tusks (<hi type="italic">shçn</hi>) on account of their shape and resemblance to horns, just as Pliny (<hi type="italic">Hist. nat</hi>. xviii. 1) also speaks of <hi type="italic">cornua elephanti,</hi> although he says, in viii. 3 (4), that an elephant’s weapons, which Juba calls <hi type="italic">cornua</hi>, are more correctly to be called <hi type="italic">dentes</hi>.<note placement="foot">The Ethiopians also call ivory <hi type="italic">Karna nage</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">cornu elephanti</hi>, and suppose that it is from horns, and not from tusks, that ivory comes (vid., Hiob Ludolph, <hi type="italic">Hist. Aeth</hi>. I c. 10).</note> <div eID="gen15051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15052" type="x-p"/> The ἁπ. λεγ.. הובנים, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> הבנים, signifies ἔβενος <hi type="italic">hebenum</hi>, ebony. The ancients obtained both productions partly from India, partly from Ethiopia (Plin. xii. 4 8). According to Dioscor. i. 130, the Ethiopian ebony was preferred to the Indian. השׁיב אשׁכּר to return payment (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">Psa 72:10</reference>). <div eID="gen15052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15053" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">Eze 27:16</reference>, J. D. Michaelis, Ewald, Hitzig, and others read אדם for  ארם, after the lxx and Pesh., because Aram did not lie in the road from Dedan and the איּים to Israel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>), and it is not till <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.18">Eze 27:18</reference> that Ezekiel reaches Aram. Moreover, the corruption ארם for אדום could arise all the more readily from the simple fact that the defective form אדם only occurs in Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="Ezek.25.14">Eze 25:14</reference>), and is altogether an extraordinary one. These reasons are undoubtedly worthy of consideration; still they are not conclusive, since the enumeration does not follow a strictly geographical order, inasmuch as Damascus is followed in Eze 27:19. by many of the tribes of Southern Arabia, so that <hi type="italic">Aram</hi> might stand, as Hävernick supposes, for Mesopotamian Aram, for which the articles mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">Eze 27:16</reference> would be quite as suitable as for Edom, whose chief city <hi type="italic">Petra</hi> was an important place of commerce and emporium for goods. רב מעשׂיך, the multitude of thy works, thy manufactures. Of the articles of commerce delivered by ארם , the red purple, embroidery, and בּוּץ (the Aramaean name for byssus, which appears, according to Movers, to have originally denoted a species of cotton), favour Aram, particularly Babylonia, rather than Edom. For the woven fabrics of Babylonia were celebrated from the earliest times (vid., Movers, II 3, pp. 260ff.); and Babylon was also the oldest and most important market for precious stones (vid., Movers, p. 266). נפך is the carbuncle (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.28.18">Exo 28:18</reference>). כּדכּד, probably the ruby; in any case, a precious stone of brilliant splendour (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.54.12">Isa 54:12</reference>). ראמות, corals or pearls (vid., Delitzsch on <reference osisRef="Job.28.18">Job 28:18</reference>). - <hi type="italic">Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>) delivered to Tyre wheat of <hi type="italic">Minnith</hi>, i.e., according to Jdg 11:33, an Ammonitish place, situated, according to the <hi type="italic">Onomast</hi>., four Roman miles from Heshbon in the direction of Philadelphia. That Ammonitis abounded in wheat, is evident from <reference osisRef="2Chr.27.5">2Ch 27:5</reference>, although the land of Israel also supplied the Tyrians with wheat (1Ki 5:11). The meaning of the ἁπ. λεγ. דם̓̀בנ̓̀ב cannot be definitely ascertained. The rendering confectionery is founded upon the Aramaean פּנק, <hi type="italic">deliciari</hi>, and the Chaldee translation, קוליא, i.e., κολία, according to Hesychius, τὰ ἐκ μέλιτος τρωγάλια, or sweetmeats made from honey. Jerome renders it <hi type="italic">balsamum</hi>, after the μύρων of the lxx; and in Hitzig’s opinion, <hi type="italic">Pannaga</hi> (literally, a snake) is a name used in Sanscrit for a sweet-scented wood, which was employed in medicine as a cooling and strengthening drug (?). Honey (from bees) and oil are well-known productions of Palestine. צרי is balsam; whether <hi type="italic">resina</hi> or the true balsam grown in gardens about Jericho (<hi type="italic">opobalsamum</hi>), it is impossible to decide (see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol</hi>. I p. 38, and Movers, II 3, pp. 220ff.). <hi type="italic">Damascus</hi> supplied Tyre with wine of <hi type="italic">Chelbon</hi>. חלבּון still exists in the village of <hi type="italic">Helbôn</hi>, a place with many ruins, three hours and a half to the north of Damascus, in the midst of a valley of the same name, which is planted with vines wherever it is practicable, from whose grapes the best and most costly wine of the country is made (vid., Robinson, <hi type="italic">Biblical Researches</hi>). Even in ancient times this wine was so celebrated, that, according to Posidonius (in <hi type="italic">Athen. Deipnos.</hi> i. 22), the kings of Persia drank only Chalybonian wine from Damascus (vid., Strabo, XV 3. 22). צמר צחר, wool of dazzling whiteness; or, according to others, wool of <hi type="italic">Zachar</hi>, for which the Septuagint has ἔρια ἐκ Μιλήτου, Milesian wool.<note placement="foot">According to Movers (II 3, p. 269), צחר is the <hi type="italic">Sicharia of Aethicus</hi> (Cosm. §108): Sicharia <hi type="italic">regio, quae postea Nabathaea, nuncupatur, silvestris valde, ubi Ismaelitae eminus</hi>, - an earlier name for the land of the Nabathaeans, who dwelt in olden time between Palestine and the Euphrates, and were celebrated for their wealth in flocks of sheep.</note> <div eID="gen15053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15054" type="x-p"/> Eze 27:19. Various explanations have been given of the first three words. ודן is not to be altered into דּדן, as it has been by Ewald, both arbitrarily and unsuitably with <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">Eze 27:20</reference> immediately following; nor is it to be rendered “<hi type="italic">and Dan</hi>.” It is a decisive objection to this, that throughout the whole enumeration not a single land or people is introduced with the copula w. <hi type="italic">Vedan</hi>, which may be compared with the <hi type="italic">Vaheb</hi> of Num 21:14, a place also mentioned only once, is the name of a tribe and tract of land not mentioned elsewhere in the Old Testament. Movers (p. 302) conjectures that it is the celebrated city of <hi type="italic">Aden</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">'dn</hi>). <hi type="italic">Javan</hi> is also the name of an Arabian place or tribe; and, according to a notice in the <hi type="italic">Kamus</hi>, it is a place in <hi type="italic">Yemen</hi>. Tuch (<hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, p. 210) supposes it to be a Greek (Ionian) settlement, the founders of which had been led by their enterprising spirit to cross the land of Egypt into Southern Arabia. For the purpose of distinguishing this Arabian <hi type="italic">Javan</hi> from Greece itself, or in order to define it more precisely, מעוּזל is appended, which all the older translators have taken to be a proper name. According to the Masoretic pointing מאוּזּה, the word is, no doubt, to be regarded as a participle <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> of אזל, in the sense of spun, from אזל, to spin. But apart from the fact that it would be a surprising thing to find spun goods mentioned in connection with the trade of the Arabian tribes, the explanation itself could not be sustained from the usage of the language; for there is nothing in the dialects to confirm the idea that  אזל is a softened form of עזל, inasmuch as they have all עזל (Aram.) and <hi type="italic">gzl</hi> (Arab.), and the Talmudic אזל, <hi type="italic">texere</hi>, occurs first of all in the Gemara, and may possibly have been derived in the first instance from the Rabbinical rendering of our מאוזל by “spun.” Even the fact that the word is written with <hi type="italic">Shurek</hi> is against this explanation rather than in its favour; and in all probability its origin is to be traced to the simple circumstance, that in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.12">Eze 27:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.14">Eze 27:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.16">Eze 27:16</reference> the articles of commerce are always mentioned before נתנוּ עזבוניך, and in this verse they would appear to be omitted altogether, unless they are covered by the word מאוזל. But we can very properly take the following words בּרזל עשׁות as the object of the first hemistich, since the Masoretic accentuation is founded upon the idea that מאוזל is to be taken as the object here. We therefore regard מאוּזל as the only admissible pointing, and take אוּזל as a proper name, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.10.27">Gen 10:27</reference> : “from <hi type="italic">Uzal</hi>,” the ancient name of <hi type="italic">Sanaa</hi>, the subsequent capital of <hi type="italic">Yemen</hi>. The productions mentioned bear this out. Forged or wrought iron, by which Tuch (<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> p. 260) supposes that sword-blades from Yemen are chiefly intended, which were celebrated among the Arabs as much as the Indian. Cassia and calamus (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Exo 30:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Exod.30.24">Exo 30:24</reference>), two Indian productions, as Yemen traded with India from the very earliest times. - Dedan (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.20">Eze 27:20</reference>) is the inland people of that name, living in the neighbourhood of Edom (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.13">Eze 25:13</reference>; see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.15">Eze 27:15</reference>). They furnished בּגדי, <hi type="italic">tapetes straguli</hi>, cloths for spreading out, most likely costly riding-cloths, like the <hi type="italic">middim</hi> of Jdg 5:10. ערב and קדר represent the nomad tribes of central Arabia, the Bedouins. For ערב is never used in the Old Testament for the whole of Arabia; but, according to its derivation from ערבה, a steppe or desert, simply for the tribes living as nomads in the desert (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">Isa 13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.2">Jer 3:2</reference>; cf. Ewald, <hi type="italic">Grammat. Arab</hi>. I p. 5). <hi type="italic">Kedar</hi>, descended from Ishmael, an Arabian nomad tribe, living in the desert between Arabia Petraea and Babylonia, the <hi type="italic">Cedrei</hi> of Pliny (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.25.13">Gen 25:13</reference>). They supplied lambs, rams, and he-goats, from the abundance of their flocks, in return for the goods obtained from Tyre. <div eID="gen15054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15055" type="x-p"/> Jdg 5:22. Next to these the merchants of <hi type="italic">Sheba</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ragmah</hi> (רעמה) are mentioned. They were Arabs of Cushite descent (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference>) in south-eastern Arabia (Oman); for   ,רעמה̔Ρεγμα, was in the modern province of Oman in the bay of the same name in the Persian Gulf. Their goods were all kinds of spices, precious stones, and gold, in which southern Arabia abounded. ראשׁ כּל־בּשׂם, the chief or best of all perfumes (on this use of ראשׁ, see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Exo 30:23</reference>; Sol 4:14), is most likely the genuine balsam, which grew in <hi type="italic">Yemen</hi> (<hi type="italic">Arabia felix</hi>), according to Diod. Sic. iii. 45, along with other costly spices, and grows there still; for Forskal found a shrub between Mecca and Medina, called <hi type="italic">Abu sham</hi>, which he believed to be the true balsam, and of which he has given a botanical account in his <hi type="italic">Flora Aeg.</hi> pp. 79, 80 (as <hi type="italic">Amyris opobalsamum</hi>), as well as of two other kinds. Precious stones, viz., onyx-stones, rubies, agates, and cornelians, are still found in the mountains of Hadramaut; and in Yemen also jaspers, crystals, and many good rubies (vid., Niebuhr, <hi type="italic">Descript</hi>. p. 125, and Seetzen in Zach’s <hi type="italic">Monatl. Corresp</hi>. xix. p. 339). And, lastly, the wealth of Yemen in gold is too strongly attested by ancient writers to be called in question (cf. Bochart, <hi type="italic">Phal</hi>. II 28), although this precious metal is no found there now. <div eID="gen15055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15056" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.23">Eze 27:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.24">Eze 27:24</reference> the trade with Mesopotamia is mentioned. חרן, the <hi type="italic">Carrhae</hi> of the Romans in north-western Mesopotamia (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.11.31">Gen 11:31</reference>), was situated at the crossing of the caravan-roads which intersect Mesopotamia; for it was at this point that the two caravan routes from Babylonia and the Delta of the Persian Gulf joined the old military and commercial road to Canaan (Movers, p. 247). The eastern route ran along the Tigris, where <hi type="italic">Calneh</hi>, the later <hi type="italic">Ktesiphon</hi>, and the most important commercial city. It is here called כּנּה (Canneh), contracted from כּלנה (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Gen.10.10">Gen 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.2">Amo 6:2</reference>). The western route ran along the Euphrates, past the cities mentioned in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.23">Eze 27:23</reference></hi>. עדן is not the Syrian, but the Mesopotamian <hi type="italic">Eden</hi> (2Ki 19:12; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.12">Isa 37:12</reference>), the situation of which has not yet been determined, though Movers (p. 257) has sought for it in the Delta of the Euphrates and Tigris. The singular circumstance that the merchants of Sheba should be mentioned in connection with localities in Mesopotamia, which has given rise both to arbitrary alterations of the text and to various forced explanations, has been explained by Movers (p. 247 compared with p. 139) from a notice of Juba in Pliny’s <hi type="italic">Hist. nat</hi>. xii. 17 (40), namely, that the Sabaeans, the inhabitants of the spice country, came with their goods from the Persian Gulf to Carrhae, where they held their yearly markets, and from which they were accustomed to proceed to Gabba (Gabala in Phoenicia) and Palestinian Syria. Consequently the merchants of Sabaea are mentioned as those who carried on the trade between Mesopotamia and Tyre, and are not unsuitably placed in the centre of those localities which formed the most important seats of trade on the two great commercial roads of Mesopotamia.<hi type="italic">Asshur</hi> and <hi type="italic">Chilmad</hi>, as we have already observed, were on the western road which ran along the Euphrates. כּלמד has already been discovered by Bochart (<hi type="italic">Phal</hi>. I 18) in the <hi type="italic">Charmande</hi> of Xenophon (<hi type="italic">Anab</hi>. i. 5. 10), and Sophaenetus (see Steph. Byz. <hi type="italic">s.v.</hi> Χαρμάνδη), a large and wealthy city in a desert region “beyond the river Euphrates.” The <hi type="italic">Asshur</hi> mentioned along with <hi type="italic">Chilmad</hi>, in the midst of purely commercial cities, cannot be the land of Assyria, but must be the emporium <hi type="italic">Sura</hi> (Movers, p. 252), the present <hi type="italic">Essurieh</hi>, which stands upon the bank on this side of the Euphrates above Thapsacus and on the caravan route, which runs from Palmyra past Rusapha (<hi type="italic">Rezeph</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.12">Isa 37:12</reference>; 2Ki 19:12) to Nicephorium or Rakka, then in a northerly direction to Haran, and bending southwards, runs along the bank of the river in the direction of Chilmad or Charmande (Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdk</hi>. XI pp. 1081ff.). The articles of commerce from these emporia, which were brought to Tyre by Sabaean caravans, consisted of מּכללים, literally, articles of perfect beauty, either state-dresses (cf. מכלל, <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.12">Eze 23:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.4">Eze 34:4</reference>), or more generally, costly works of art (Hävernick). The omission of the copula ו before בּגלומי is decisive is favour of the former, as we may infer from this that 'בגל is intended as an explanatory apposition to מּכללים. גּלומי תכלת ורקמה, cloaks (גּלום connected with χλαμύς) of hyacinth-purple and embroidery, for which Babylonia was celebrated (for proofs of this, see Movers, pp. 258ff.). The words which follow cannot be explained with certainty. All that is evident is, that 'ואר 'בּחבלים חב is appended to בּגנזי בּרומים without a copula, as 'בּגלומי וגו is to בּמּכללים in the first hemistich, and therefore, like the latter, is intended as an explanatory apposition. חבלים does not mean either cloths or threads, but lines or cords. חבשׁים signifies literally bound or would up; probably twisted, i.e., formed of several threads wound together or spun; and ארזים, firm, compact, from Arab. <hi type="italic">arz</hi>, to be drawn together. Consequently 'גּנזי בּרומים וגו can hardly have any other meaning than treasures of spun yarns, i.e., the most valuable yarns formed of different threads. For “treasures” is the only meaning which can be assigned to גּנזים with any certainty on philological grounds, and בּרומים, from בּרם, Arab. <hi type="italic">brm , contorsit</hi>, is either yarn spun from several or various threads, or cloth woven from such threads. But the latter would not harmonize with חבלים. Movers (II 3, pp. 263ff.) adopts a similar conclusion, and adduces evidence that silk yarn, bombyx, and cotton came to Tyre through the Mesopotamian trade, and were there dyed in the splendid Tyrian purples, and woven into cloths, or brought for sale with the dyeing complete. All the other explanations which have been given of these difficult words are arbitrary and untenable; not only the Rabbinical rendering of גּנזי בּרומים, viz., chests of damask, but that of Ewald, “pockets of damask,” and that proposed by Hartmann, Hävernick, and others, viz., girdles of various colours, ζῶναι σκιωταί. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.25">Eze 27:25</reference> the description is rounded off with a notice of the lever of this world-wide trade. שׁרות cannot mean “walls” in this instance, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.5.10">Jer 5:10</reference>, and like שׁוּרות in <reference osisRef="Job.24.11">Job 24:11</reference>, because the ships, through which Tyre became so rich, could not be called walls. The word signifies “caravans,” after שׁוּר = Arab. <hi type="italic">sâr</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.9">Isa 57:9</reference>), corresponding to the Aramaean שׁירא. מערבך might be regarded as an accusative of more precise definition: caravans, with regard to (for) thy bartering trade. At the same time it is more rhetorical to take מערבך as a second predicate: they were thy trade, i.e., the carriers of thy trade. What the caravans were for the emporia of trade on the mainland, the ships of Tarshish were for Tyre, and these on the largest sea-going ships are mentioned <hi type="italic">instar omnium</hi>. By means of these vessels Tyre was filled with goods, and rendered weighty (נכבּד), i.e., rich and glorious. - But a tempest from the east would destroy Tyre with all its glory.
entries.41477e7cbe33b39d197337ce5ed454da788afb80: <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26-Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:26-36</reference> <div eID="gen15056" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Destruction of Tyre</title> <div sID="gen15057" type="x-p"/> Eze 27:26. <hi type="italic">Thy rowers brought thee into great waters: the east wind broke thee up in the heart of the seas.</hi> Eze 27:27. <hi type="italic">Thy riches and thy sales, thy bartering wares, thy seamen and thy sailors, the repairers of thy leaks and the treaders in thy wares, and all thy fighting men in thee, together with all the multitude of people in thee, fell into the heart of the seas in the day of thy fall.</hi> Eze 27:28. <hi type="italic">At the noise of the cry of thy sailors the places tremble.</hi> Eze 27:29. <hi type="italic">And out of their ships come all the oarsmen, seamen, all the sailors of the sea; they come upon the land,</hi> Eze 27:20. <hi type="italic">And make their voice heard over thee, and cry bitterly, and put dust upon their heads, and cover themselves with ashes;</hi> Eze 27:31. <hi type="italic">And shave themselves bald on thy account, and gird on sackcloth, and weep for thee in anguish of soul a bitter wailing.</hi> Eze 27:32. <hi type="italic">They raise over thee in their grief a lamentation, and lament over thee: Who is like Tyre! like the destroyed one in the midst of the sea!.</hi> Eze 27:33. <hi type="italic">When thy sales came forth out of the seas, thou didst satisfy many nations; with the abundance of thy goods and thy wares thou didst enrich kings of the earth.</hi> Eze 27:34. <hi type="italic">Now that thou art wrecked away from the seas in the depths of the water, thy wares and all thy company are fallen in thee.</hi> Eze 27:35. <hi type="italic">All the inhabitants of the islands are amazed at thee, and their kings shudder greatly; their faces quiver.</hi> Eze 27:36. <hi type="italic">The traders among the nations hiss over thee; thou hast become a terror, and art gone for ever.</hi> - The allusion to the ships of Tarshish, to which Tyre was indebted for its glory, serves as an introduction to a renewal in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26">Eze 27:26</reference> of the allegory of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.5-Ezek.27.9">Eze 27:5-9</reference></hi>; Tyre is a ship, which is wrecked by the east wind (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.48.8">Psa 48:8</reference>). In Palestine (Arabia and Syria) the east wind is characterized by continued gusts; and if it rises into a tempest, it generally causes great damage on account of the violence of the gusts (see Wetzstein in Delitzsch’s commentary on <reference osisRef="Job.27.1">Job 27:1</reference>). Like a ship broken in pieces by the storm, Tyre with all its glory sinks into the depths of the sea. The repetition of בּלב in <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.26">Eze 27:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.27">Eze 27:27</reference> forms an effective contrast to <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.25">Eze 27:25</reference>; just as the enumeration of all the possessions of Tyre, which fall with the ship into the heart of the sea, does to the wealth and glory in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.25">Eze 27:25</reference></hi>. They who manned the ship also perish with the cargo, - ”the seamen,” i.e., sailors, rowers, repairers of leaks (calkers), also the merchants on board, and the fighting men who defended the ship and its goods against pirates, - the whole <hi type="italic">qâhâl</hi>, or gathering of people, in the ship. The difficult expression בּכל־קהלך can only be taken as an explanatory apposition to אשׁר בּך: all the men who are in thee, namely, in the multitude of people in thee. Eze 27:28. When the vessel is wrecked, the managers of the ship raise such a cry that the <hi type="italic">migreshōth</hi> tremble. מגרשׁ is used in Num 35:2 for the precincts around the Levitical cities, which were set apart as pasture ground for the flocks; and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.2">Eze 45:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.48.17">Eze 48:17</reference>, for the ground surrounding the holy city. Consequently מגרשׁות cannot mean the suburbs of Tyre in the passage before us, but must signify the open places on the mainland belonging to Tyre, i.e., the whole of its territory, with the fields and villages contained therein. The rendering “fleet,” which Ewald follows the Vulgate in adopting, has nothing to support it. <div eID="gen15057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15058" type="x-p"/> Eze 27:29. The ruin of this wealthy and powerful metropolis of the commerce of the world produces the greatest consternation among all who sail upon the sea, so that they forsake their ships, as if they were no longer safe in them, and leaving them for the land, bewail the fall of Tyre with deepest lamentation. השׁמיע with בּקול, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.26.7">Psa 26:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.19">1Ch 15:19</reference>, etc. For the purpose of depicting the lamentation as great and bitter in the extreme, Ezekiel groups together all the things that were generally done under such circumstances, viz., covering the head with dust (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.7.6">Jos 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.12">1Sa 4:12</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Job.2.12">Job 2:12</reference>) and ashes (התפּלּשׁ, to strew, or cover oneself, not to roll oneself: see the comm. on Mic 1:10); shaving a bald place (see <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.18">Eze 7:18</reference> and the comm. on Mic 1:16); putting on sackcloth; loud, bitter weeping (בּמר, as in <reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference>); and singing an mournful dirge (Eze 27:32.). בּניהם, <hi type="italic">in lamento eorum</hi>; ני contracted from נהי (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.17-Jer.9.18">Jer 9:17-18</reference>; cf. הי, <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.10">Eze 2:10</reference>). The reading adopted by the lxx, Theodot., Syr., and eleven Codd. (בּניהם) is unsuitable, as there is no allusion to sons, but the seamen themselves raise the lamentation. The correction proposed by Hitzig, בּפיהם, is altogether inappropriate. The exclamation, Who is like Tyre! is more precisely defined by כּדמּה, like the destroyed one in the midst of the sea. דּמּה, participle <hi type="italic">Pual</hi>, with the מ dropt, as in 2Ki 2:10, etc. (vid., Ges. §52. 2, Anm. 6). It is quite superfluous to assume that there was a noun דּמּה signifying destruction. 'בּצאת עזב has been aptly explained by Hitzig; “inasmuch as thy wares sprang out of the sea, like the plants and field-fruits out of the soil” (the selection of the word השׂבּעתּ also suggested this simile); “not as being manufactured at Tyre, and therefore in the sea, but because the sea floated the goods to land for the people in the ships, and they satisfied the desire of the purchasers.” Tyre satisfied peoples and enriched kings with its wares, not only by purchasing from them and paying for their productions with money or barter, but also by the fact that the Tyrians gave a still higher value to the raw material by the labour which they bestowed upon them. הוניך in the plural is only met with here. - Eze 27:34. But now Tyre with its treasures and its inhabitants has sunk in the depths of the sea. The antithesis in which <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.34">Eze 27:34</reference> really stands to <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.33">Eze 27:33</reference> does not warrant our altering עת into עתּ נשׁבּרתּ, as Ewald and Hitzig propose, or adopting a different division of the second hemistich. עת is an adverbial accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.57">Eze 16:57</reference> : “at the time of the broken one away from the seas into the depth of the waters, thy wares and thy people have fallen, i.e., perished.” עת נשׁבּרת, <hi type="italic">tempore quo fracta es</hi>. נשׁבּרת מימּים is intentionally selected as an antithesis to נושׁבת מימּים in Eze 26:17. - Eze 27:35. All the inhabitants of the islands and their kings, i.e., the inhabitants of the (coast of the) Mediterranean and its islands, will be thrown into consternation at the fall of Tyre; and (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:36</reference>) the merchants among the nations, i.e., the foreign nations, the rivals of Tyre in trade, will hiss thereat; in other words, give utterance to malicious joy. שׁמם, to be laid waste, or thrown into perturbation with terror and amazement. רעם פנים .tnemezama dna, to tremble or quiver in the face, i.e., to tremble so much that the terror shows itself in the countenance. - In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.27.36">Eze 27:36</reference></hi> Ezekiel brings the lamentation to a close in a similar manner to the threat contained in Ezekiel 26 (vid., <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.21">Eze 26:21</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ezek.27"/> <div eID="gen15058" type="x-p"/>

               <ns0:p n="25">25 The ships of Tarshish <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">The Ships from all parts of the Sea, which came to thee, and traded with thee, praised thee, boasted of thee.</ns0:note> did sing <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Had their songs of praise, which were made to commend thy state.</ns0:note> of thee in thy market <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">As Mariners in the Ports, where they arrive usually do with Mirth, and Songs entertain one another, so at <ns0:hi>Tyre.</ns0:hi>

               <ns0:p n="31">31 And they shall make themselves utterly bald <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It was the custom of the Heathen, to either pull off with their hands, or cut off the hair of their heads in great mourn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ings, which God forbad to his people, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 18.28. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 14.1.1. thus do <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> mourners in baldness express their sorrow, and despair.</ns0:note> for thee, and gird them with sackcloth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Another usual Ceremony of mourners well known to all.</ns0:note>, and they shall weep for thee with bitterness of heart <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">It shall be a hearty mourning, not a counter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />feit one, this referring to the inward grief, the next bitter wailing refers to the outward expressing it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> bitter wailing.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:105" />32 And in their wailing <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">In their sorrowful speeches of <ns0:hi>Tyrus.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> they shall take up <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Into their mouths, or with a composed, significant, and comprehensive form of speech to shew much grief in few words.</ns0:note> a lamentation for thee, and lament over thee, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> What <ns0:hi>city is</ns0:hi> like <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">A few years since no city like her in beauty, riches, glory, and joy, now none like her in all the contraries.</ns0:note> Tyrus, like the destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Now no more <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> the flou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rishing, the renowned, the Mart of Nations, and the stately built; but now the destroyed, the silent overwhelmed with grief, which was full of Songs.</ns0:note> in the midst of the sea <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Alas! what was once her safeguard, is now her grave, what enricht her once hath now swallowed all up at once.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 When thy wares <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Brought home from all Coasts.</ns0:note> went forth out <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Were Landed, brought on shoar for the Mart.</ns0:note> of the seas thou filledst <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">There was enough to supply to the full.</ns0:note> many people <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Numerous, stately, sumptuous Nations, though their prodigality was great, thou furnishedst them, hadst wares rich, and stately enough for all of them.</ns0:note>; thou didst enrich the kings <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Such influence had thy vast Trade, that not only meaner men and subjects, but Kings themselves were made more wealthy by it.</ns0:note> of the earth <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> All Kings of the known World, or Kings of Nations far off, as well as neighbouring Kings.</ns0:note> with the mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />titude of thy riches <ns0:note n="s" place="margin">The greatness of thy Trade, the varie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty of thy wares brought from all parts, were thy own riches, and enricht all thou didst Trade with; Kings were enricht by Customs, and Tolls paid to them by the enriching their subjects, who thereby were fitter to pay Taxes, or by furnishing their treasuries with all the peculiar Treasures of Kings, the rare, and precious Jewels, which they esteem; and since we know some Kings did Trade too, by this <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> increast their Wealth.</ns0:note>, and of thy merchan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dise.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 In the time <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">So soon as, or ever after the unhappy day.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="35">35 All the inhabitants of the isles <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Strictly and in a larger sense the Sea-Coasts.</ns0:note> shall be astonished <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Wonder<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, it ever should be effected, that <ns0:hi>Tyrus</ns0:hi> should fall.</ns0:note> at thee, and their kings shall be sore afraid <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing how they are much less able to resist, and defend themselves<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and not knowing where that mighty Conqueror would next trie his Arms, and Fortune.</ns0:note>, they shall be troubled <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">They shall not be able to conceal the discomposure of their mind, but in their countenance a trouble made up of grief, fear, and indignation, grief for their Friends, fear for themselves, against that cruelty, and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />humanity, which without respect to any thing dear to man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kind, ruined the glory of the World, destroyed, what could not be repaired by all the riches, and wisdom, and bounty of the <ns0:hi>Babylonish</ns0:hi> Kingdom.</ns0:note> in <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> countenance.</ns0:p>
